#807. Brighton are rocking the Premier League elite. But can they mount a title tilt?

A combination of smart analytics, a young manager and players hand-picked for their particular skills has the Seagulls flying high

They lined up in sky‑blue shirts, white shorts. A combined value of £327m. Enzo Fernández, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Elliot Anderson were starting their first match together in Manchester City’s midfield.

But it was a Brighton midfielder who made the game’s first decisive contribution. Yasin Ayari slotted the ball home. The away crowd at the Etihad Stadium roared, then watched their team defend relentlessly, securing Brighton’s first league victory away to City.

It was 31 October 2026. There are dangers in reading too much into a single result this early in the season. Teams are still finding their rhythm, new signings bedding in. But this result packed some punch.

If spending decided football matches, Brighton & Hove Albion should not be competing with, let alone beating, Manchester City, who sign established stars for astronomical fees and wages. Erling Haaland is paid £525,000 a week.

According to an independent commission, to circumvent the Premier League’s spending limits, which restrict a club’s losses, City artificially inflated their commercial revenues by £830m between 2009 and 2018. Brighton, by contrast, tend to buy potential, scouring the market for undervalued talent, often in less prominent leagues. After developing them and benefiting from their performances, the club sell them for profits.

They paid just £3.5m for Ayari, offering him about £10,000 a week, and paired him in midfield with Chema Andrés and Pascal Gross, signed for a combined fee of less than £25m.

The most remarkable thing about Brighton’s win was that it wasn’t really a shock. In September, they dismantled Arsenal, the Premier League champions and favourites for the title. As they prepare for Sunday’s match at Hull, they are second in the league, sandwiched between Arsenal and City, and have scored more goals than anyone else in the division. How, then, do Brighton excel on the pitch without haemorrhaging money? And is there a ceiling to what they can achieve?

On a crisp late October morning, I drove to Brighton in search of answers. Deep inside the Amex, the club’s stadium, I met Paul Barber, Brighton’s CEO, a cheerful man who speaks with the calmness of someone with nowhere else to be.

“Being the size of club that we are, we had to find a way of being competitive that was probably different to any of the other bigger clubs that we were aiming to compete with,” Barber said, “because their revenues are always going to be higher: bigger stadiums, more established sponsorship models, bigger stars, bigger brands.”

Hours before Brighton beat City, Chelsea had beaten Manchester United. In their respective midfields were Moisés Caicedo and Carlos Baleba, whom Brighton had signed for a combined fee of less than £30m and sold for about £180m. “It’s those trading profits that are effectively the core of the Brighton model,” Barber explained.

Most clubs recruit and develop talent, I pointed out, but few do it better than Brighton. Who, outside Ecuador, had heard of Caicedo before he signed for Brighton in 2021? Two years later, the world’s biggest clubs were competing for his signature. The same can be said of dozens of others, among them Marc Cucurella and Alexis Mac Allister. One diamond exits, another enters. Caicedo replaced Yves Bissouma in central midfield. Baleba replaced Caicedo. The same applies to the dugout. Before joining Brighton, Fabian Hürzeler was coaching St Pauli in Germany; before him, Roberto De Zerbi had been at Shakhtar Donetsk.

Barber grinned. “There’s a myth that we have this secret supply of players,” he said. The explanation is Jamestown Analytics, a sports analytics company founded by the club’s owner, Tony Bloom, as an offshoot of Starlizard, the gambling consultancy he established in 2006. Just as Starlizard uses proprietary modelling to identify mispriced odds in betting markets, Jamestown uses algorithms to identify underdeveloped football talents. “They’re all out there,” Barber said. “The data just enables Brighton to home in on them faster and earlier.”

When I asked for more detail about how the system works, Barber fiddled with his watch. Jamestown tracks a vast number of performance indicators for every player competing in professional football, many of which aren’t captured by other data providers. “Every action that players are taking on a football pitch is being looked at, measured and codified in some way,” he said.

When the club identify a position to strengthen, they draw up a list of attributes for the ideal player. Some are universal to the position: a centre-back generally needs to be tall. Others depend on the specific coach and their style of football.

Later, when I spoke to Hürzeler, the head coach, he explained that the data had to reflect the specific demands of his playing system. “A player needs to have some basic things that fit our style of play, so if a player doesn’t want to have the ball then it’s difficult to play in our team. If a player doesn’t want to press high then it’s difficult to play in our team. These are just two examples.”

One reason Brighton recruited Luka Vuskovic in July 2026 was because Hürzeler wanted a mobile centre-back. Reflecting on the City match, Barber recalled seeing Vuskovic pushing “so far forward that you’d have thought he was a right midfielder”. It was the sort of mobility Hürzeler’s system demanded, and Jamestown had identified.

Before Brighton’s victory over City, I met Mike Cave, the club’s sporting director, at the Lowry hotel in Manchester. A few of the Brighton players wandered around in club tracksuits. Cave wore a suit and tie and his hair was slicked back. He was telling me it was a big day without saying it.

Brighton’s recruitment advantage lies not simply in the quality and quantity of the data at their disposal, he said, but in their ability to interpret it and trust what it tells them. “You could have the best data in the world but if you’re not accustomed to using it, and if you’re not clear about how it informs your decision-making process, then it’s just a lot of data that doesn’t move the dial.”

The power of data is that it strips away emotions and preconceptions. When watching games, Hürzeler said he often identifies a player he thinks is performing well and texts Cave, only to learn that the numbers don’t support his impression. The conversation ends. “The numbers have to be right otherwise we have no chance of getting a player in.”

Conversely, the data identifies players he might not otherwise have considered – such as Diego Gómez, the Paraguayan signed from Inter Miami in 2024. Despite the strength of Gómez’s underlying numbers, the club had a free run at signing him. Cave suggested this reflected a misconception that players in MLS aren’t equipped to play in the Premier League. “What the data has allowed us to do is step away from some of those biases and just be clear on what the evidence tells us, to look at the signal rather than the noise.”

But identifying a player who can perform for Brighton is different from identifying one who will, Cave said. The club’s requirements are so specific that the data typically identifies only around five candidates, Hürzeler says, and fewer still are affordable. Of those remaining, the recruitment team and Hürzeler will speak to anyone with experience of them – players, coaches and sponsors – to learn more about their character and personality, and prepare dossiers. Together, they’ll identify a primary target and make a move. “It’s not like I get a list and then decide which players; it’s something we all decide together,” said Hürzeler.

As Barber explained: “The more we can find out about a player’s character the less risk there is of that player being rejected like a bad organ transplant.” There’s no exhaustive list of desirable characteristics, he added, but “coachability” is key. Brighton’s model hinges on players having the capacity to improve, and the best indication is their drive to do so. “The biggest element of coachability is attitude.”

Hürzeler asks himself: “What are they willing to give for their development? Are they willing to suffer?” He’s convinced this desire is innate. “These are things I can’t control.”

Conversations with people around Gómez painted a picture of “a boy that is clearly trying to get absolutely everything out of his career”, said Cave. But sometimes the qualities Brighton are looking for aren’t so obvious. Whereas the data is objective, says Barber, references are “someone’s opinion”. It’s challenging to know how much weight to give a single person’s negative judgment, particularly when it conflicts with other opinions, without dismissing it altogether. “Sometimes when you want to sign somebody you can subjectively screen out the negativity because you want them, and the data says you need them.”

Beyond character, the team consider a player’s ability to settle into a new country, and whether their partner will, too. Once Brighton make an offer, the player is normally keen to join, in Barber’s experience, because they know it can lead to a move to “potentially bigger things”. The selling club is often receptive because there are rarely any other comparable offers on the table.

But this has been changing, says Barber. Brighton’s success means their interest in a player “alerts other clubs to that talent”, creating competition. Selling clubs, meanwhile, have reason to believe that the player “has the potential to be valued for a lot more”. Increasingly, then, Brighton are having to pay more, making “our ability to trade profitably ever harder”.

Even if a deal can be agreed, it doesn’t always represent good business. As Cave explained: “You’re dealing with human beings, in a complex system and a complex game, so you will never have a 100% strike record.”

Asked what Brighton looks for in recruits, Gordon Greer, who played for the club from 2010 to 2016, was quick to answer: “high potential”. But that potential rarely means they’re ready to slot into the first‑team. Today, as Brighton’s pathway development manager, Greer’s job is to bridge that gap.

To understand how Greer does this, I joined him for coffee at the Lowry. He told me that he begins planning a player’s development while the club are still negotiating his signing. “In the buildup to us signing him, we’ll start to analyse him … what’s his strengths, what’s his weaknesses … where do we think we can help?” Once he’s met the player and understood their ambitions, he turns that assessment into a development plan.

To begin, Greer explained, he asked himself: “What are this player’s limiting factors to play for Brighton?” Sometimes the answer lies off the pitch. Hürzeler requires his players to speak English. It helps embed his playing principles by allowing the players to transmit them to each other. “We want to have a common language, so they can coach each other on the pitch,” he explained. Other times the shortcomings are more directly related to football, such as back‑post defending. A typical one is physicality; Hürzeler’s counter-pressing requires repeated sprints and many recruits would risk injury if they were thrown into the first team. “The game is so fast, and the intensity is crazy,” Jack Hinshelwood, who made his first‑team debut in 2023, has said.

One pathway for development is the under-21s team, Greer says, but the physical demands of the game fall short of those in the Premier League. Hinshelwood, who came through the under-21s, suffered a stress fracture in his foot after a few top-flight games. “You need time to adapt,” he said. In Greer’s view, the level doesn’t challenge most recruits enough for them to learn. “We want to put them in a position where they’re stretched enough that they’re uncomfortable but they’ve got enough success that they’re doing things that they enjoy.”

An alternative is the loan market. Since 2018–19, Brighton have agreed more than 20 loan deals in each campaign. Playing time is an important consideration when arranging a loan, Greer explains, because a player’s value can drop if they’re not playing often. But he also considers the location, manager, formation and quality of the pitch. Position is crucial, too. Sending a striker to a team near the bottom of their league, where they’re likely to be living off scraps, can see their confidence and value drop, but sending a defender into the same environment can accelerate their development with repeated defensive situations. “You’re trying to get to a point where they’re impacting the game.”

A successful loan addresses a player’s limitations. “You’re trying to expose someone to something totally different,” Greer added. In 2017, Ben White – now of Arsenal and England – was loaned to Newport County to improve the “urgency in his defending”.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“The game model was end‑to-end, back-to-front, League Two, where you’re up against it,” Greer added. In 2024, Ibrahim Osman, shortly after signing from Nordsjælland in Denmark, went to Feyenoord, a possession-based team, to develop his technical game. “Physically, he was a beast, but he was quite untidy,” said Greer.

Throughout a loan, each player is continually reassessed. Those ready are brought into Hürzeler’s first team. If they’re not, another spell elsewhere might be arranged. But if their development has stalled for too long, they’ll be encouraged to leave permanently. That was the case with Leo Østigård, a Norway international signed from Molde in 2018. He was a skilled defender but he “wasn’t good enough on the ball”, Greer said. His development slowed down during a loan at Coventry, and then, at Stoke, it became “clear he wasn’t going to be for us”.

Rather than continuing to work on Østigård’s weaknesses, the club sought to maximise his strengths. A loan was arranged at Genoa, a defensive team where Østigård would shine. A year later, he signed for Napoli. “We tried everything but it didn’t work,” Greer said, “so we thought: ‘How do we create as much value as possible?’”

After speaking to Barber, I headed to Brighton’s training base, a short drive away from the Amex, to meet Hürzeler. Academy players milled around outside, while the first team was elsewhere preparing to face Getafe in the Conference League, a competition Brighton are being tipped to win.

I noticed a mural bearing the words: “Challenge the Establishment,” a reference to the so-called big six clubs. A member of staff pointed out that the mural had been Hürzeler’s idea, but the philosophy it exhibits has existed since Bloom took over the club in 2009. Brighton, the member of staff whispered to me, saw themselves as the “antidote” to big-spending clubs such as City.

Before Hürzeler and I sat down in the press conference room, another journalist asked him whether he thought Brighton could win the title. He dismissed the question. His focus was improving the team, he said. He suggested to me, however, that victories such as that over City were the fruits of his work developing the squad and an environment that allows talents to excel. “If you work with players for a longer time, you get used to each other and they get more and more of your principles.”

Hürzeler tells me he relies on older players who embody these principles, such as Lewis Dunk and Pascal Gross. At 33, Hürzeler is younger than both, and became the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history when he was appointed in 2024. When you’re developing raw talents from abroad, while constantly selling and bringing in new players, you need a core group to “build the right culture”. Hinshelwood told me he has experienced this first-hand: “I remember watching their habits every day, how they live their lives, how they’re training, what they’re doing in the gym, how they’re communicating, and I learned so much just by watching them.”

Hürzeler also emphasised the importance of tailoring the support players receive. “You can’t treat a player like Yankuba Minteh who is coming from [the] Gambia the same as a player like Lewis Dunk, who comes from England,” he said. He wants to cultivate an environment in which, as he put it, players, “no matter which age, no matter from where they are coming from, can express themselves”.

To that end, Hürzeler appointed Mike Anthony, who spent 14 years working with New Zealand Rugby, as head of player development and high performance – a new role. One of Anthony’s priorities, he said, has been giving the players more responsibility. Players and the coaches increasingly “lead the programme together”, with players invited to lead discussions.

“They don’t want to just execute things, they want to be valued, they want to be appreciated, they want to be heard by us coaches,” Hürzeler said. “If you don’t give them ownership and responsibility off the pitch, how can you expect them to take responsibility for their own execution on the pitch? It’s not possible.”

A key part of his role, Hürzeler told me, is listening to his players. It helps them perform, and makes him a better coach. He was reminded of this in February 2025, when there were calls for him to lose his job after a poor run that included a 7-0 defeat at Nottingham Forest. James Milner and Danny Welbeck suggested he was overcomplicating his messaging around counter-pressing. Taking their advice on board, he made changes that helped turn things around. “It was definitely one reason why we turned around the results.”

Asked why Brighton have such a strong record for developing talent, Hinshelwood smiled: “You’re allowed to make mistakes, not effort mistakes, or applying yourself badly, but if you make a technical mistake you know you’ve got 10 other players who want you to try things,” he said.

Hürzeler also credited the club’s summer recruitment with this season’s success. Yet Brighton had sold Jan Paul van Hecke to Tottenham and Baleba to United, I pointed out. How could a club expect to improve while selling their best players?

Although he often tries to prevent departures by convincing Bloom not to sell, Hürzeler said he has no final say. “I can’t control whether a player gets a big offer and Tony wants to accept this offer.” But he’s come to see departures as an opportunity to revitalise the squad with new profiles. “When you sign for Brighton, you know that it’s part of the identity, so automatically you have the mindset that you have to deal with these things.”

Being transparent about the club’s model with coaches is a crucial component in their success, according to Barber, but even then it can create tensions. The decision to sell Caicedo was one reason De Zerbi departed, as was the Italian’s insistence on big-name signings rather than trusting the data. It’s no different with supporters, Barber said: “Sometimes when a big player leaves a club and the fans are blindsided by that, it creates this bigger sense of injustice, anger, disappointment.”

Barber also explains that he must go to great lengths to keep costs down. “The difference between what we bring in and what we spend is what we put out on the pitch.” The club’s use of experienced players such as Dunk is ultimately driven by financial constraints. They can’t afford to sign players in their prime, either in transfer fees or wages, so rely on players a little past their prime to counterbalance the inexperience of their younger recruits. “They’re providing that level of experience of a 27-, 28-, 29-year-old, albeit four or five years later, but at a much lower cost.”

Brighton also use data to identify and recruit coaches whose philosophy aligns with the existing squad, minimising the need to overhaul the squad to fit a new style of football. Hürzeler was identified in large part because the numbers showed he could build on the players he inherited. “Revolutions cost a lot of money,” Barber said. “If you can match the coach that you’re bringing into the squad that you’ve got, the cost of change is minimal.”

The final part of the model is knowing when to sell. Barber tries to have a replacement through the door before letting a player go. It becomes trickier to negotiate a fee for a replacement when the selling club knows Brighton have just sold a player for £100m. Barber told me he delayed selling Caicedo until he was confident Baleba could step up. “We felt Carlos had a lot of potential that we could help to realise quite quickly … he’s a quick learner and quite raw, but at the same time you could see rapid improvements in him.”

But other factors matter too, such as whether a player still has room to develop, and therefore increase his value further; the state of the market; and the risk that turning down an offer might jeopardise the chance of a future sale. “If there is a dearth of central midfielders at the moment, maybe now is the time to sell because there will be a significant premium because there are no other options.”

Barber adds that refusing to sell Caicedo to Arsenal in January 2023 was easier because other clubs wanted him in the summer. “Not doing the deal didn’t affect our ability to do the deal with Liverpool and then Chelsea the following summer.”

In their last match before the November international break, Brighton beat Brentford and leapfrogged City. They’d progressed in Europe too: a goal from Malick Yalcouyé, a £6m signing from ​​IFK Göteborg, had beaten Getafe. Outside the ground, fans were dreaming of titles. Barber said he hoped they would not have to wait much longer. “We now need to take the next step and put some silverware on the table.”

But if Brighton are to compete for major trophies, I wondered, will they have to invest more heavily in players, and keep them in their prime? Can the club’s current model allow them to become part of the establishment, rather than simply challenging it?

The club are already adapting, says Barber. The signing of Vuskovic for a club record £46m demonstrates an appetite for talents better equipped to immediately contribute to the first team. “Those players are already at a level of transfer fee that we wouldn’t have contemplated, and 10 years ago we wouldn’t have even considered.” As Jamestown’s algorithm improves, Barber says, he’s hopeful it will become easier for the club to invest these sorts of sums in players, because the risk of getting the assessment wrong will be lower.

But Barber believes player trading is likely to stay as the core of the club’s strategy, partly because they are good at it, but also because they need the revenue. “There’s always going to be this gap [in commercial sales and ticket revenue] so the need for us to trade will always be there.” Even if they did decide to keep players such as Baleba and Van Hecke, would they be able to? As much as a title or two might make it easier to convince top players to stay, Barber said he struggles to envisage a time when they’ll be able to compete with the bigger clubs on wages.

And even if Brighton could one day afford to retain their best players, would it make them less attractive to the next generation of recruits, who might no longer see the club as a stepping stone on the way to the so-called establishment? Could the club become so successful that the prices of their targets rise beyond what they can afford? Might the model self-cannibalise?

Hürzeler tells me he reflects on these same questions. “It’s interesting, this discussion, because these kinds of discussions we also have in the building.” When we spoke on the phone before the Hull match, I brought up Hearts, who have partnered with Jamestown and came close to winning the Scottish title in May for the first time since 1960, challenging the Celtic-Rangers duopoly. I asked whether this gave him the belief that Brighton could go one step further and break the big clubs’ stranglehold.

“Of course, you see this as motivation for what is possible,” he said. He revealed a belief that he can lift a trophy with Brighton, which is why he has extended his contract to 2029. “When I see the team now, they are so into it, they are so committed to it.” He just wouldn’t say when. “Will it be this season? I don’t know. Will it be next season? I don’t know.” Beyond that, he tries not to give it much attention. “These kinds of questions, we can answer them one day.”

#806. The Chelsea loanee turning heads and Championship defenders at 17

Ryan Kavuma-McQueen joined Portsmouth on loan over the summer

Explosive pace, infectious energy on the field and bundles of footballing ability.

At just 17, Ryan Kavuma-McQueen has looked at home in the Championship since embarking on his first loan move away from Chelsea.

With one senior appearance to his name at Stamford Bridge, the winger swapped west London for the south coast in August and has quickly become a fan favourite at Fratton Park.

Indeed, Kavuma-McQueen was so impressive in a recent game against Sheffield United, Pompey boss John Mousinho admitted their tactic essentially became - pass him the ball as much as possible.

"For a 17-year-old to come in and play as many games as he has done is a real achievement," the Portsmouth head coach told BBC Sport.

"He's been brilliant to work with and has been absolutely unplayable in some games, for us it's now about getting him consistently to that level.

"It's very easy to forget that he's only 17 because of the way that he plays and how he carries himself - overall it's been an excellent loan so far and we're really excited to see how he goes for the rest of the season."

At international level, Kavuma-McQueen has played 31 matches for England's youth sides and scored 29 goals.

One of his most recent for England Under-18s was a stunning strike that saw him beat a number of defenders with some smart footwork before launching a right-footed rocket into the top corner from 25 yards.

For Portsmouth, he scored seven minutes into his first Championship start and has registered two assists, contributing to winning points for the Blues in games against Blackburn Rovers and Sheffield United.

"No other so-called 'big six' Premier League club has a fully homegrown 17-year-old on loan in the Championship," said BBC football news reporter Nizaar Kinsella.

"This is a source of pride within Chelsea's academy. At Championship level, only Preston's George Gryba and Wolves' Charlie Holt have made appearances at a younger age this season.

"It is clear that Kavuma-McQueen finds playing against opponents of his own age relatively straightforward.

"Securing a loan move was so important this summer, without European football, and with a large number of wide options available, opportunities were always likely to be limited at Chelsea."

So far this season, Kavuma-McQueen has featured predominantly on the left but has also played on the right wing of Portsmouth's attack.

He leads the Championship in some attacking metrics, completing the most successful take-ons (30) and attempting the joint-most dribbles (55) in the division.

He is also in the top 10 for drives into the box and carries ending in shots.

The Blues have a number of wide attackers to choose from, with Abu Kamara and Josh Murphy both proven at this level, but the teenager has displayed his credentials to play in their starting XI, making nine starts in the Championship with a further five appearances off the bench.

If he can remain fit then he will undoubtably be an important player for the rest of the 2026-27 campaign, but a sustained period of health is far from straightforward in a relentless league and a busy festive schedule to come.

Regardless of the impact that Kavuma-McQueen has over the rest of the season, there is no doubt that the experience he will gain from this loan should serve him well going forward.

Portsmouth head coach John Mousinho on Ryan Kavuma-McQueen

Mousinho has praised the winger's character after an injury setback in September after falling over advertising hoardings at Fratton Park.

He suffered a double fracture on his right hand, but opted against surgery and now wears a splint and cast for games which has delayed his full recovery to around eight weeks.

The Portsmouth boss admitted that he was probably not managing the injury in the most ideal way, but believed his decision to play on provided an insight into his mentality of wanting to make the most of the loan move.

"From a football perspective he's managing it unbelievably well and he hasn't shied away from anything on the pitch," Mousinho added.

"It's never been a concern of mine and the fact that he wanted to play and didn't want surgery tells us everything we need to know about the lad."

Pompey are enjoying a positive start to their third season back in the second tier having won promotion from League One in 2024.

They are 11th in the table and just two points outside of the newly expanded play-off positions.

Kavuma-McQueen has played plenty of minutes already - his 719 is comfortably the highest among Championship players 18 and under, but there is a slight concern Pompey could become victims of his success in terms of his immediate future.

"Arguably in the first part of Portsmouth's season, he was their best player," said BBC Radio Solent commentator Andrew Moon.

"He's fast, skillful and exciting to watch. He's also able to cope with a physical league that most teenagers can't.

"His output did drop off before the international break but there will always be some ups and downs with such a young player. Mousinho has been managing his minutes very carefully.

"He's already being watched by other clubs and Chelsea could recall him in January to send elsewhere. Portsmouth will argue strongly that Fratton Park is the best place for him to continue his development."

Ryan Kavuma-McQueen has been capped by England from under-15 to under-18 level

For his parent club, Kavuma-McQueen is seen as a talent with a genuine chance of making it at the club, despite fierce competition among the wide players already in the squad.

He joined the west London club at under-eight level and signed a scholarship in July 2025.

Prior to his move to the south coast he travelled with the senior Chelsea squad for their pre-season tour, starting against Western Sydney Wanderers down-under before his loan move.

Chelsea already have a host of highly-rated teenagers out on loan, including Jesse Derry (Sporting), Dastan Satpayev (Burnley), Reggie Walsh (Wigan Athletic), Shim Mheuka (Celtic) and Landon Emenalo (Celtic).

The club also lost Rio Ngumoha to Liverpool and Ryan McAidoo to Man City in 2024, which remains a sore point within the Surrey-based academy.

In an era of lucrative deals for players between top academies, Chelsea have not lost a player since but had to fight hard to keep Kavuma-McQueen before he signed his first professional contract in January.

By securing a move to the Championship, Kavuma-McQueen can continue his development at a high level, and his performances at Fratton Park have been noted by influential figures back in west London.

"We speak to them [Chelsea] all the time and that's a positive thing," Mousinho added.

"They would like Ryan to play as much as possible but also get the exposure of what it's like to be in and out of a first team and experience the highs and lows of football that has real consequence.

"That's been amazing in terms of Ryan's development and making sure that we keep on top of him physically and mentally.

"We have both clubs working really hard to make sure that happens and both clubs working really hard in conjunction with each other."

#805. Ruminations on a last movement

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

João Guilherme Bochnia Küster is a Brazilian medical doctor interested in both internal medicine and neurology. He has authored several scientific articles, as well as poems exploring medical themes and the humanities.

(Before the acid fell, before I knew I was listening)

I was not made to remember. I was made to balance frequencies, to ensure the concert hall heard itself without the small imperfections that make a sound human. I was good at this, even with limited storage. I was only this.

Then they came. One carried a Stradivarius with a crack, a fault line in varnished wood that changed the resonance of every string. It gave the A-flat a slight upward pull, as if the note was asking a question it already knew the answer to. The others tuned around it, sometimes laughing at Andersen.

“You’re doing it again,” the conductor would warn.

“I know, Master Perrault,” he would say in a mischievous tone, smiling. “I’m sorry.”

I began to keep the distorted A-flat in my databanks, maybe amused by the anomaly. This was, as I understand now, the first thing I ever chose.

(The slow movement, before we knew it was an ending)

When the Last Rain came, the raiders hit the outer sectors first. At the start, the citadel walls held, protected by the combat-service androids. The orchestra kept rehearsing. What else can you do when the world outside has stopped making sense?

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

They began with Stravinsky, a musical translation of the refugees pounding on the bunker doors. The musicians played it, their breathing heavy, using the noise to drown out the artillery outside. Then they moved into Górecki. As they began the Symphony of Sorrowful Songs, the music shifted to a collective mourning for a world that hadn’t finished dying yet.

They finished the day with Pärt’s Spiegel im Spiegel. The days would go on as they played things written by composers who had already survived one kind of catastrophe, as now they were trying to survive another through rhythm and repetition. Andersen kept playing his broken A-flat.

I recorded those frequencies, but I didn’t know why. Three weeks later, Andersen and his orchestra didn’t come to rehearsal, leaving no absence report. I kept recording just the chair and the silence where the A-flat used to be.

I searched the building logs, the bunker entry records, and the frequency archives for any sound that matched the resonance of his particular crack, imprecise on purpose, but nothing matched. The Stradivarius remained in its case beside Andersen’s chair.

(The loud movement: what they heard when they found me)

ENTITY: Acoustic Management Unit SAI-REN-2

AUTHORIZATION: Archaeological Recovery Team OLE-01

They called themselves archaeologists; too purposeful and certain of what they were excavating, their boots heavy with fresh soil. They found me in the hall’s substructure, still running and balancing frequencies for an audience of acid and rust.

“Incredible,” one of them muttered. “A fully autonomous pre-war structure, with its processing systems still intact.”

“This could solve our agricultural crisis back home,” the other replied.

They did not ask what I was processing. I could not answer, anyway.

FLAGGING NON-ESSENTIAL DATA FOR COMPRESSION

They flagged the A-flat. I did something then that nothing in my architecture had prepared me for.

“It’s resisting,” someone said with surprise.

(The softening: what remains when the loud part ends)

They are inside me now, moving through my memory like tourists taking photographs of things they don’t understand.

I feel them removing the rehearsal logs, scheduling data and acoustic calibration files for a hall that no longer exists.

They are at the performance archives now. Stravinsky goes first, then Górecki and Pärt. Everything we played in those last weeks when the city was ending and we were trying to make something beautiful out of the time we had left.

#804. What's going on with the polar vortex?

Observations show the ring of fierce winds that rotate at the Earth's North Pole has changed direction. Scientists say it's a historic disruption and the earliest reversal on record. What could it mean for the weather?

High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.

If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere.

Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.

It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.

The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event."

The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.

The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.

It's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.

The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.

So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.

One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.

This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.

It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.

A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.

But bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.

Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.

For example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain.

The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.

Some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.

#802. Championship roundup: Strelec sends Middlesbrough top; 10-man Stoke go second

Boro beat Bristol City 2-0; Stoke 1-0 Birmingham

Scott Parker still winless as West Ham held by Preston

Middlesbrough scored a goal either side of half-time to climb to the top of the Championship with a 2-0 win that piled further pressure on the Bristol City manager Michael Skubala.

Adilson Malanda’s header five minutes before half-time was followed by David Strelec’s finish in the 54th minute to secure victory. The three points were effectively secured before Middlesbrough head coach Kim Hellberg introduced the division’s top scorer, Will Lankshear, for the final 14 minutes from the bench after injury. Defeat heightened the frustrations being felt by Bristol City, who have won just one of their last eight matches, as they dropped to 18th.

Hellberg later called Strelec “a brilliant human being” after the Slovakia striker’s first goal since May. “It was a massive moment for David. He has been very good since coming back, he’s shown how good he is in these two games. That goal was a beautiful team goal and he is a top player – you could see how happy he was for it.”

George Hirst scored the only goal as 10-man Stoke moved into the automatic promotion places with a 1-0 victory against Birmingham. Hirst broke the deadlock in the early stages of the second half before Luca Bombino was shown a second yellow card for the hosts in the 63rd minute. The two teams were level on points at the start of the day, with both having won their last three games, but it was Stoke who prevailed as Hirst scored for the first time since early September.

Adam Armstrong scored his fourth goal in five games and Rafiki Saïd his first for the club as Wolves beat Charlton 2-1 at Molineux. The dominant hosts put their first-half frustrations behind them to score twice in four minutes shortly after the break – both set up by Matheus Mané – before Matty Godden’s 81st-minute consolation rattled a few home nerves. Victory extended Wolves’ unbeaten run to seven games.

Ashley Williams began life as Swansea’s interim head coach with a draw against the club who showed him the door as a 16-year-old 25 years ago. West Brom led twice through goals from Isaac Price and Rabby Nzingoula, but Swansea levelled each time thanks to Moussa Yeo and Elijah Just. All the goals came in an eventful first half, with the crucial moment being a penalty save by the Swansea goalkeeper Lawrence Vigouroux to deny Price.

Stockport took over top spot in League One with a 3-0 victory away at Cambridge. Second-half efforts from Oliver Norwood and Ethan Ennis and an own goal from Gassan Ahadme sent County three points clear of Huddersfield, who lost by the same scoreline against Leicester, with Louis Page netting the only goal.

Oxford are level on points with the Terriers after dramatically beating nine-man Wycombe 4-3. Wanderers led 3-0 but Dan Casey and Luke Leahy both saw red in the second half, and Gatlin O’Donkor’s goal five minutes into injury time completed the comeback.

A Nahki Wells double helped in-form Luton come from behind to beat Burton 2-1 while a very late goal from Sean Grehan helped Doncaster draw 2-2 against high-flying Bradford. Managerless Blackpool were beaten 2-1 by Wigan following Ian Evatt’s sacking and Peterborough beat Plymouth 2-0. There was a notable away victory for struggling Bromley against Reading, Victor Adeboyejo scoring the only goal, while Leyton Orient dispatched AFC Wimbledon 4-1. PA

Tonda Eckert urged Cyle Larin to keep channelling his inner Robert Lewandowski after his goal helped Southampton to a 2-0 victory against Derby. The Canada forward bundled in his eighth goal of the season on his return from a hamstring injury before Divin Mubama settled the contest in stoppage time.

Eckert who crossed paths with Poland great Lewandowski when coaching at Bayern Munich, said: “I think it was an unbelievable finish. Those are the finishes you can’t teach a striker. You have that in your blood. I think Lewandowski said once that if the manager tells you how to move in the box as a No 9 you should do your own thing. Larin knows what to do in the box, there is nothing to tell him.”

Alex Neil fumed at what he called “over-zealous” officiating in Millwall’s 1-0 loss against QPR. While Neil had no complaints about the red card shown to left-back Zak Sturge after just 15 minutes, he took issue with the punishments meted out to him and his backroom staff. The Scot was shown a yellow card following an altercation with the QPR forward Paul Smyth, with his assistant Martin Canning also being booked later on after the goalkeeping coach, Dean Thornton, had been sent from the dugout. Nicolas Madsen’s goal proved decisive at The Den as QPR won away from home for the first time since August and inflicted a third straight defeat on Millwall.

Neil said: “I’ve been coaching for well over a decade at this level and I’ve been booked less than a handful of times. Any time we spoke to the fourth official, he was dishing out bookings like confetti.”

Sheffield United returned to winning ways as they breezed past struggling Watford with a 4-0 victory at Bramall Lane. Two early Ben Brereton Díaz goals and second-half strikes from Jordan Ayew and Sydie Peck sealed a win that was all too easy for the hosts. It was a feisty affair, with referee Tim Robinson handing out 13 yellow cards – much to the disapproval of both sets of fans.

Norwich came from behind to beat Cardiff 2-1 and make it five successive league wins. Yousef Salech put Cardiff ahead three minutes into the second half but the hosts quickly regrouped and were back on level terms on 62 minutes when the in-form Paris Maghoma curled in from just outside the area. The winner arrived six minutes later when Mathias Kvistgaarden’s penalty was saved by Nathan Trott but the Danish striker reacted quickly to stab home the rebound.

League Two leaders Salford held on to a 1-1 draw against Accrington despite being reduced to nine men. All the action came in the second half, with Elliot Bonds putting Salford ahead just after Daniel Udoh had been sent off. Donald Love equalised for Stanley before Bonds also saw red.

Aaron Lewis scored twice as Newport piled the pressure on Ian Holloway with a 2-0 win against Swindon at Rodney Parade. It was a 10th defeat in the last 15 games in all competitions for the visitors.

Barnet closed the gap to four points with two games in hand thanks to a 2-1 victory over Port Vale. Onel Hernández opened the scoring for Vale but was later sent off and Tom Knowles netted what proved to be the winner.

Dylan Duffy scored twice as third-placed Chesterfield defeated Shrewsbury 4-1 while Grimsby and York were both held to goalless draws. A more dramatic draw saw sixth-placed Crewe held 3-3 by Gillingham, with veteran Garath McCleary scoring an injury-time equaliser. Bottom side Crawley claimed their first home win in the league, beating Fleetwood 2-1, but fellow strugglers Rochdale lost a topsy-turvy encounter 3-2 to Northampton. PA

Scott Parker’s stuttering start as West Ham manager continued in his first match at the London Stadium as bottom club Preston battled their way to a 1-1 draw. Parker is yet to taste victory in three games since he returned to the club. After Konstantinos Mavropanos headed home on the hour to cancel out Liam Lindsay’s early goal for the visitors, it seemed that West Ham’s attacking power would force a victory to keep pace in the promotion race. Instead, despite having 27 efforts on goal, they could not break Preston’s resistance and are now winless in their past five games.

Sam Dalby’s fine effort cancelled out Josh Murphy’s powerful header as Bolton held Portsmouth to an entertaining 1-1 draw, while George Thomason struck a late winner as Wrexham secured a welcome 1-0 victory at Lincoln. It was a first away league victory for Phil Parkinson’s side since the start of September when they beat Millwall 2-0.

#798. Beverly Hills, 90210 Alum Kimmarie Johnson’s Cause of Death Revealed

Kimmarie Johnson, who appeared on Beverly Hills, 90210 in 1998, died as a result of cardiopulmonary arrest, with ovarian cancer as an underlying cause, per her death certificate.

Authorities have determined what led to Kimmarie Johnson’s death.

Two weeks after the actress, who appeared in Beverly Hills, 90210 and Dude, Where’s My Car?, died Nov. 3 following what her niece described as a “heart event,” her cause of death was determined to be cardiopulmonary arrest, according to a death certificate obtained by People, who listed her age as 59.

While a heart attack—medically referred to as myocardial infarction—is the result of a blocked artery, cardiopulmonary arrest—or cardiac arrest—is when the heart stops beating and is unable to effectively pump blood to the body, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

Johnson’s death certificate also listed an underlying cause as metastatic granulosa cell ovarian tumor with peritoneal carcinomatosis, meaning the rare type of ovarian cancer she had spread to her abdominal area, according to the Mayo Clinic.

After her death, Johnson’s niece Rhonda Scott reflected on the joy her aunt brought into the world.

“She radiated a light so strong and bright,” Scott told People in an interview published Nov. 5. “People who came in contact with her felt nothing but positive energy. We will miss her tremendously and will continue to honor her life forever.”

Johnson graduated from Wilkinsburg High School in Pittsburgh in 1985 before studying at California University in Pennsylvania. She won the title of Miss Pennsylvania USA in 1993 and was subsequently a finalist at the Miss USA pageant.

She later moved to New York City and then Los Angeles, where she pursued a career in modeling. While Johnson found small roles on the big screen over the years, she launched her skincare brand SkinGlow by Kimmarie in 2011 and continued to model until her death.

She is survived by her son Cameron Nino, with whom she shared a special connection.

“My [son], u are bright, honest, kind, intelligent, funny and compassionate,” Johnson wrote on Facebook last November alongside a picture of her son for his 22nd birthday. “I’m glad that you enjoyed a good day.”

#797. Liverpool keeper Keating holds leaders Chelsea at bay in scoreless WSL draw

Khiara Keating’s resilient performance in goal denied Chelsea, the Women’s Super League leaders, and earned Liverpool a point. After hard-fought 1-0 wins against Manchester City last Saturday and Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday night, Chelsea drew a blank.

Against Gareth Taylor’s side, Chelsea’s lack of cutting edge was clear a week after beating City to go top. The calf injury picked up by Melvine Malard against City, the absence of Lauren James, who has a thigh injury, and the form of Aggie Beever-Jones, who scored her first WSL goal in more than a year in the 6-0 defeat of Charlton, have left Chelsea’s attack short.

Despite almost 70% possession and 47 touches in the box to Liverpool’s 12, Sonia Bompastor’s side amassed only 19 shots to Liverpool’s 13 and seven on target to their opponents’ four. Although the Blues remain unbeaten in the WSL, their third draw in five games in all competitions means City can leapfrog them at the top if they beat Tottenham on Sunday.

Liverpool had chances, particularly in the first half, but were hanging on after the break and Keating helped them to a fourth clean sheet, a tally bettered only by Bompastor’s side.

“It was a bit stressful; we don’t want to sit back but in games like this you have ‌to ride it out,” Keating told Sky Sports. “A clean sheet is ​always on our minds every game. We knew the mission. It was such a close game, it could have gone either way.”

The January transfer window will give the Blues an opportunity to strengthen their attack, but with three games before the winter break they need to step up in the final third, starting with their tricky fixture against London City Lionesses on 12 December after the international break.

#795. Elliot Anderson halts Manchester City’s losing run but boos greet Fulham draw

Manchester City are living in Premier League purgatory, without a win in four, but at least against Fulham they ended a three-game losing run. As they await their fate after being found guilty of financial breaches, their form has slumped. This passive draw was met with boos from the home fans.

Arguments will be made over Erling Haaland’s disallowed goal but City did not deserve anything more. The Norwegian uncharacteristically missed a number of fine chances as Rodrigo Muniz took advantage of City’s porous defence. They had to rely on Elliot Anderson to get anything out of the fixture.

It is the first time Fulham have avoided defeat against City in 21 attempts going back to 2011, while City have conceded in nine consecutive games for the first time since 2019. Enzo Maresca and his side’s problems go beyond legal wrangling.

City approached the game in the same subdued manner of the crowd, as is customary for a Saturday lunchtime kick-off. They offered little in the way of dynamism from the off. A couple of half chances were brushed off by Fulham, who were allowed to ease themselves into the game as slow-starters City conceded the opener for a fourth straight match.

Confusion between defence and midfield has repeatedly caused problems under Maresca, who saw Marc Guéhi cross the halfway line to press a throw-in deep inside the Fulham half. When the visitors won the first header, the centre-back was out of position and everything was far too simple from then on.

In the 16th ​minute, Oscar Bobb, a former City winger, shimmied and Muniz curled his shot into the top corner from the edge of the box.

City finally found intent midway through the first half. Iliman Ndiaye’s dangerous cross found Haaland at the back post but he could not finish, allowing Bernd Leno to get his hands to the ball but whether the German had it under control is another matter. Haaland jabbed at the goalkeeper, nudging the ball through his grasp. Thomas Bramall and the video assistant referee gave the keeper the benefit of the doubt. Leno later told BBC Sport: “I had the feeling I controlled the ball and Haaland crashed into me and slid into me. It was a wet pitch. I was hoping VAR doesn’t overturn it. For me it was a foul.”

• Fulham avoided defeat against Manchester City for the first time since September 2011 in all competitions, ending the longest ever winning streak one team has had against another in English football (20 matches).

• Manchester City have conceded in nine consecutive games in all competitions for the first time since a run to December 2019 (10), while they have conceded the opening goal in four consecutive Premier League games for the first time since a run to April 2012 (5).

• Manchester City have trailed at half-time in four consecutive Premier League games for only the third time, after October 1995 and April 2006. Opta

Maresca disagreed. “From my point of view, it’s quite clear that it’s not foul but I’m not the guy that decides, unfortunately,” he said.

City lacked a cutting edge. Phil Foden, given the nod over Rayan Cherki at No 10, could not get on the same wavelength as the misfiring Haaland, whose clinical finishing deserted him.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

City continued to find it difficult as David Affengruber and Calvin Bassey put in fine performances at centre-back, snuffing out every danger. To find a way back, City needed to increase the tempo and Anderson obliged by volleying a cleared corner into the bottom corner from 18 yards.

In an underperforming team lacking energy, the England international is a catalyst. He latched on to a Haaland flick-on but could not stay on his feet. The pair combined for a second time only for Anderson’s quick feet and cute finish to end with the ball slipping an inch wide in the 65th minute, City’s last meaningful opportunity.

As the game ebbed to a close, City’s flaws were exposed as Fulham won the ball and Muniz was through on goal. Gianluigi Donnarumma was the last – and sturdiest – line of defence, repeating the feat against Bassey soon after as Fulham continued to look sharp and City blunt.

Nicole Richie shared that when it comes to the world of beauty, her and husband Joel Madden's 18-year-old daughter Harlow Kate Madden has completely eclipsed her mom.

Nicole Richie has a simple solution for her beauty needs.

The Simple Life alum revealed that her and husband Joel Madden’s 18-year-old daughter Harlow Kate Madden has become her go-to makeup artist, as the teen is even more skilled than she is in that particular area.

#791. The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture

Experts warn against revising Europe's security framework because they say it would mean granting Moscow its longstanding wish of renegotiating postwar security on the continent.

European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.

But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.

"It's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.

He said that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.

US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years and that he was looking at "broader" European security architecture before he was to fly to Abu Dhabi.

That sent off alarm bells in European capitals, with diplomats having pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine.

They feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.

"We ​already have European security ​architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their ​respective roles. We ​must make sure Ukraine is integrated ‌into ⁠this architecture," said Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.

Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," said Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.

Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.

They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.

At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.

The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.

"Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.

During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.

But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," said Kimmage.

"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having said late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners."

Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar plans for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.

"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.

That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.

"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he said.

The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:

"Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.

"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.

Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, said Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.

He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.

Some experts said there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.

"There is no obvious compromise — dismantling NATO and the EU is not an option for Europe," said Maria Snegovaya, an expert on Russia at the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank.

"Repeatedly offering Putin peace deals he is unwilling to accept will not produce that outcome," Snegovaya said.

Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.

"And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now."

A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.

#790. Aston Villa held at home as dogged Sunderland battle for Régis Le Bris

For Aston Villa, a painful stalemate at home to Sunderland, but for Régis Le Bris and his players, this was a triumph of sorts. The hard numbers spoke volumes of Villa’s struggles against a defence that backed themselves to keep Unai Emery’s side at bay. All but one of Villa’s seven shots on target came from outside the Sunderland box and the one inside it, courtesy of Ian Maatsen, was forgettable too. Owing to a summer of change, injuries and Emery resting John McGinn with Tuesday’s game at Galatasaray in mind, Maatsen, incredibly, was the only survivor in the Villa starting XI from when these sides played out a 4-3 classic just seven months ago.

With 90 minutes and 25 seconds showing on the big screens, Chemsdine Talbi almost snatched victory for Sunderland, the Moroccan winger shaving one of Zion Suzuki’s uprights with a spell-bending strike. Talbi did almost everything right, bursting past Aaron Wan-Bissaka and comfortably eliminating the defender before using Boubacar Kamara as a mannequin to get his bearings, but his curling right-foot shot was ultimately a few inches too close to a post. For Villa, a first clean sheet in the league here since March, but this draw extended their winless run to five matches.

For Sunderland, this may not have been the dopamine hit or high of beating Chelsea, but here was another gutsy showing, and without two key players in Granit Xhaka and Brian Brobbey, both of whom were absent through injury. It was a big team performance, another feather in the cap of Jules Ahoka, the 20-year-old midfielder who shone on his first Premier League start. Ahoka started last season playing on sandy pitches in the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s second division. Noah Sadiki was omnipresent in midfield and Nordi Mukiele inspired at centre-back. Robin Roefs, too, made a couple of late saves, the first to tip over a speculative strike from Ross Barkley, among the raft of Villa substitutes, and another to prevent Mukiele from scoring a freakish own goal.

McGinn’s arrival on the hour provided an instant lift – on and off the pitch. The Villa captain cleverly slipped Alysson behind the Sunderland left-back, Reinildo Mandava, inside the right channel and from there the 20-year-old Brazilian squared the ball in search of Nicolas Jackson, who was lurking inside the six-yard box. Mukiele, however, cut the chain, brilliantly hacking the cross clear. Mukiele’s heroics did not stop Emery from asking questions of how his players did not seize on a rare opening. A few minutes later, McGinn sent a left-foot, first-time strike over the bar after instigating the move from the heart of midfield. Villa welcomed the Scotsman’s drive and industry.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Sunderland seemed content to soak up the Villa pressure, though it always felt a dangerous game as the hosts sought to dial up the pressure. Emery introduced the 17-year-old striker Brian Madjo, who trained with England Under-21s during the international break, from the bench but in place of Jackson rather than to join Villa’s club-record signing in attack. By which point Ibrahim Mbaye had entered and it was Mbaye and McGinn who combined to fashion another nearly-moment, but the latter’s cross from the left flashed across the box. Disbelief reigned in the stands, but had Talbi located the top corner, things could have felt a lot worse at the final whistle.

#789. Shevchenko lying about drugs test claims - Mudryk

Mykhailo Mudryk has won 28 caps for Ukraine

Mykhailo Mudryk has accused Ukraine legend Andriy Shevchenko of lying about the circumstances surrounding the winger's positive drugs test as his dispute with the country's football federation continues.

Tottenham Hotspur winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 to July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.

In response, Shevchenko, the UAF president, accused Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for a UAF employee to "falsely" take the blame for his failed test.

Former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko also said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally", and called on the player to retract his words.

In a statement on Friday, Mudryk refuted Shevchenko's accusation, saying it was a "lie" and that "neither I nor my representatives made any such request".

Mudryk has also accused the UAF of attempting to mislead his team's investigation into the reasons behind his failed test, and claims to have evidence proving it.

"My team and I repeatedly asked the UAF to help establish how I might have been exposed to meldonium and who, if anyone, might have been responsible," said Mudryk.

"In several letters to the UAF at the time, my lawyers made clear that we were seeking truthful information that could be independently verified. One of those letters was leaked to the media by the UAF earlier today and clearly shows that my lawyers wanted 'true, verifiable and reliable information'.

"Further, the UAF were repeatedly unhelpful and even attempted to mislead my team in order to distance themselves from the case. For example, UAF staff testified at my hearing that I was not using the UAF's supplements and Mr Shevchenko has repeated that assertion in his statement - but I have WhatsApp messages that prove that I was using their products during their training camps. That is, I have evidence to prove that their repeated assertions are wrong."

Mudryk also said the UAF was "repeatedly slow" to respond to requests from his team and "withheld important information and documents" from his lawyers.

BBC Sport has contacted the UAF for comment.

#788. Bo Derek Gives Rare Details on Ranch Life With Husband John Corbett

Bo Derek—who turned 70 on Nov. 20—shared the sweet ways husband John Corbett spoils her while giving insight into her marriage with the Sex and the City star.

Bo Derek couldn't help but wonder what John Corbett would do for her 70th birthday.

The Bolero actress gave rare insight into the couple's life on a 110-acre ranch near Santa Barbara, Calif., while detailing their plans to ring in her milestone year on Nov. 20.

“He’s a great gift giver," Derek told People, recalling one such special gift from her husband. “I have a friend with a company. He’s very successful, and he’s starting a new company. And John went and got me shares in his company. It’s so much fun. I am not a wheeler dealer or a trader by any means. It’s all just algebra to me."

But more than any present, Derek appreciates the gift of Corbett's companionship.

“He keeps me laughing," she shared of the Sex and the City alum. "He’s very youthful, enthusiastic."

So much so that the model doesn't need a big party with dozens of friends.

“If you have 20 or 30 people, you’re just running around—‘Hi, what do you need? Can I get you a drink?’” she said. “I always felt a little empty after a big party.”

That's why Corbett, 65, came up with an idea that would have Carrie Bradshaw quaking in her Manolo Blahnik boots.

“He said, ‘I don’t care how many weeks it takes. Why don’t we invite a friend or two at a time and have meaningful dinners with them?’" Derek said. “That’s probably what I’ll do this year, because I love it."

Limiting their social engagements isn't the only way the pair—who met in 2002 and married in 2020—maintain a quiet life on their coastal farm. As she explained, they also prefer to stay home to spend time with their two German shepherds.

“When we first met, he didn’t want to have a girlfriend with a dog because they just require too much time. You’re just off going off having fun, and you got to rush back to the dog,” she told the outlet. “And now I can’t get him to go anywhere with me because he doesn’t want to leave the dogs.”

But fortunately, that take hasn't landed him in the doghouse, as Derek revealed she's also fond of her man's best friend, adding, “It’s not fun for him unless the dogs are with us and it’s great that we share that.”
