#711. ‘Yellowjackets’ Creators on Closing Their Survival Story, Killing Characters and Thoughts on Spinoffs: “This Was Meant to Be the Final End”

Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson hope to leave viewers satisfied when the fourth and final season of the Showtime hit releases its series finale: "We do feel like this closes the book, and I think that's important."

[This story contains mild spoilers from the premiere of Yellowjackets season four.]

The end is near for Yellowjackets. The fourth and final season of Showtime‘s hit survival story has begun, and the weekly drop of final episodes will send viewers on a wild ride as they ruminate on life, death — and the meanings behind those bizarre post-Yellowjackets dreams. If it’s any consolation, the creators have those dreams, too.

“Life just keeps getting wider, and the show has been part of that. It’s been an expression of that width and an agent in creating that width,” Bart Nickerson, chatting with his co-creator wife, Ashley Lyle, tells The Hollywood Reporter of the last near-decade making the hit Showtime series. The pair initially planned for five seasons, but when the Paramount renewed Yellowjackets for a fourth and final season, the creators pivoted. Related Stories NEXT BIG THING Jasmin Savoy Brown Bids Farewell to 'Yellowjackets' and Finds Her Way to 'Hadestown' Lifestyle The Paramount+ Black Friday Deal Gets You Two Months for Less Than a Latte

“For us,” says Lyle, “it was about storytelling momentum and, with the uncertainty of the industry right now, let’s just finish a story if we can. We took a good, hard look at it. If we had felt like we couldn’t get it done, we probably wouldn’t have taken the chance. But it felt like we could.”

What they deliver is what viewers have been waiting for when the survivors of the Yellowjackets plane crash that began the series are rescued and returned home in the season four premiere. Following the teens as they reassimilate into life in New Jersey — while learning how to live with the murders and cannibalistic acts they harbor; the things they did to survive those months in the wilderness — delivers a fascinating watch and full-circle return to where this story began.

Below, Lyle and Nickerson dive into making the final season and what to expect, including the pain of killing off characters while always knowing who would survive in the end. They also explain why they aren’t interested in spinoffs — because they’re ending the story with a period, not an ellipses: “We do feel like this closes the book, and I think that’s important. I think that’s part of the contract with the audience — that you’re telling a complete story.”

We have been waiting for this rescue season. When we spoke with you two way back in the beginning of all of this, in your heads, you had envisioned Yellowjackets as a five-season show, and here you are ending with four seasons.

How big of a pivot was this to wrap up the show earlier than you planned?

LYLE Ultimately, as we were breaking this season, we realized that it was workable. It came down to: Do we potentially overstay our welcome? Of course, when you’re making television, there’s always a risk that you will not get another season. So we realized at a certain point that there was a much more high-octane version of this season that could accomplish all the things that we really hoped to accomplish when we first conceived of the show.

Coming off of the third season, we always knew we wanted to get the girls back home. Then we always knew in the adult timeline that we wanted things to start turning in on itself amongst these women in their relationships. And it did feel like we had hit that pivot point at the end of season three. So we just ended up going full steam ahead; burden the hand. The ability to tell a complete story, to finish it on our own terms, is something we’re incredibly grateful for. We hope everyone feels a sense of satisfaction with this final season.

Given the narrative of viewers dropping off after two seasons of a show, did you feel like season three was the hardest point to keep your audience, and did that affect what you wanted to do going into four?

BART NICKERSON To be honest, I didn’t know that was a thing — that audiences drop after two season. I think, in some respect, through the entire run of the show, there is, as it turns out, a gift in being, tremendously insecure and scared. (Laughs.) Every script we’ve ever written, even if we’re just going to our writers group, you have so much of your personal self-worth and the quality of that script, you kind of live and die on every piece of feedback. Although it sounds insane, the stakes of making a season of television are almost a little intellectual — you don’t ever stand in front of the audience and hear them reacting to your thing. Because the stakes are always so high, it wasn’t about: How do we keep this going? Or: People didn’t like this, how do we address that? At the end of the day, you just have to make the story you’re trying to make for better or for worse. And some may say for worse! (Laughs.)

LYLE I don’t really understand the metrics of how they’re counting viewership at this point. I’m not sure anybody does. I think they said season three was the most watched, but some of that, I’m sure, is people catching up on Netflix. For us, it was about storytelling momentum and, with the uncertainty of the industry right now, let’s just finish a story if we can. And we took a good, hard look at it. If we had felt like we couldn’t get it done, we probably would have taken the chance. But it felt like we could.

As the storytellers, you have a huge ensemble. So many stories to tell. What were some of the biggest challenges knowing that this was it? That you had a finite number of episodes left.

NICKERSON Yes, just that in and of itself [is the challenge]. We love television. We love telling television stories, and we love our characters and want them all to have a full, complete arc. Then there is the reality only having so many pages and so many minutes on screen. So it’s about how to be as efficient as possible, and that has always been a challenge. We’ve always wanted each episode, each season, each scene to have a beginning, middle and an end. So it’s about, how do you tell these stories with efficiency but also arc? That has always been an incredible challenge.

Did it leave more things on the cutting room floor? Anything you can share now that didn’t work or make the show?

LYLE Not necessarily in a macro sense for this season. Every episode, we’re always over time. We’ll sit with the editors and pull out 10 seconds at a time to get it under 60 minutes. You’re always cutting. That was the case in season one. That was the case in season two. Sometimes you go back and go, “Remember when that scene existed?” And the fact is that it was sort of telling you that it didn’t need to be there. So I think the process kind of works itself out as you go.

LYLE That’s a question for Paramount Skydance!

NICKERSON Having one less season [I don’t think changes that], because we came to an end that was meant to be the final end. There are always ideas you haven’t had yet. So, never say never. But there isn’t something where it’s like, because we had one last season, we could come back and revisit that.

Do you two feel like you are closing the Yellowjackets book with this ending? No ideas for a tangent or a right turn in any way?

LYLE We do feel like this closes the book, and I think that’s important. I think that’s part of the contract with the audience — that you’re telling a complete story. I suppose in this day and age, there’s a never-say-never quality to this question, but at the same time, we wanted to tell a complete story. We wanted it to feel like the audience had been on the full ride. And hopefully, that there’s a lot of emotional satisfaction in the resolution that we find.

NICKERSON At the end of the day, there’s a level on which, if you’re telling a story about survival, you’re telling a story about death, and that means there has to be an end, because that’s what you’re confronting — the end-end. And, what does it mean when it’s over? I don’t think it would be possible to tell a satisfying ending if it didn’t feel like the ending … of everything … ever. (Laughs.)

You come out swinging with the season four premiere jumping right into the rescue timeline. You could have built your way up to it. Can you talk about why you wanted to lead with it, and fill in the gaps from the past as the season goes?

LYLE That is a storytelling paradigm we’ve always been drawn to: not necessarily the “what happens” but the “why.” That was a big part of season one with the question of whether or not they engage in cannibalism. There were people who said, did you ever consider teasing that out? And we’re like, “No.” We wanted to put it in the pilot, because to us, the most interesting thing wasn’t whether or not they’d do it. It was, why did they do it? How did they get there? What is the context for it?

Similarly, with this season, it was a clearing of the decks, a reset in a way that could set up this season as a standalone season. And again, it wasn’t if they get rescued, it’s how and why, and what happens in the aftermath?

We would talk in the writers room, now that we’ve got four timelines or (let’s just make things a little more complicated for ourselves!), in terms of post-rescue, pre-rescue and present day. And it felt like what happened in the interim between Natalie’s distress call and them getting rescued could serve much more effectively as a little bit of mystery. Because to us, the more important emotional heartbeat of this season was going to be the post-rescue: how they were coping with and the different ways they would personally strategize how they would handle the reintegration. That was a much more interesting question for us at this point.

So much has happened to these characters over the course of the series, but it’s also been almost a decade since you two started developing this show. Do you feel like you also have grown with the show, in terms of how you wanted to end it and what you want to say in the end?

NICKERSON Speaking for myself, yes, tremendously. It would be difficult for me to fully articulate what I mean, but so much of this story is a result of stuff that’s been churned up and has continued to churned up. I always say the best compliment that people will give us about the show is, “I just started watching Yellowjackets. My dreams have been so messed up!” This idea that there is a deepness to the show.

I’ve had some bizarre dreams while watching these screeners!

NICKERSON (Laughs.) That’s been our life for nine years! Just weird dreams. (Laughs.) I feel like life just keeps getting wider, and the show has been part of that. It’s been an expression of that width and an agent in creating that width.

This show is about surviving and about death. There have been so many big deaths along the way. We still feel Juliette Lewis’ exit and last season, you took so many of them away! Fans are always reacting. How much did you take the fans into account when you thought about who is going to survive this season?

LYLE We didn’t. I don’t think we can, because, ultimately, if we were trying to please some segment of the audience, we’re going to displease another. We have to write it for ourselves and use that as a guiding light and principle. It’s a fool’s errand to try to do fan service, especially when you’re planning how to end a show.

NICKERSON The first time we met with Julie Plec, who gave us our first job in television, it was a couple days after a big character death in Vampire Diaries. It was like, “Oh, my God. I can’t believe you killed this person!” She got very serious and was like, “It’s my job to service the story before I service what the fans think they want.”

Because, ultimately, when I’m rooting for a character, I have this relationship with them. I’m not really thinking about the story. I’m thinking about the character and my relationship to them. In order to give the fans something of value, you have to keep your eye on what you’re trying to build and not necessarily on how it’s going to be received.

Your characters are like your babies. Is there a death that still sits with you or any character you wish you still had around to play with?

LYLE I think that speaks to what Bart was saying. They’re all difficult. But one that always comes back around as being rough for everybody involved on set was when we killed Coach Scott last season. Steven [Krueger] knew very early on — we go way, way, way back. He was like, “It’s time. I’m surprised I lasted this long.” There are moments where, man, you miss the character, you miss having that actor on set. But at the same time, it had to happen.

NICKERSON And that’s one of the moments I am most proud of. Every time we watched, it was such an incredible performance by both of them [Krueger and Sophie Thatcher]. It was amazing. The whole thing to watch the Natalie character born in this ultimate sacrifice that she’s making for somebody else, but it’s also a grisly, violent act. I so miss that character. But, what are we doing if it’s not trying to create those moments?

I know those calls to your departing actors have been difficult along the way, but I imagine dying in the final season is different. You probably get some cheering. It’s like a badge of honor.

Did you always know who would be the final girl(s), or did it change along the way?

NICKERSON My only hesitation is that, on the path, you investigate different things. But, no, it was at the beginning. At the beginning, this was how we were going to do it.

LYLE We kicked the tires a lot. But we really ended up in the place we thought we would.

NICKERSON Yeah. Some of the particulars changed. Ultimately, the meaning of it has, for me at least, shifted. But yeah, we actually did end up where we thought we would.

I know you can’t talk spoilers. But is there anything you want to tease… will dead characters return? Will we ever see that lost episode? Any surprises in store?

NICKERSON We’re not allowed to say! We want to reveal everything. We just want you to see it!

You have always talked about having big beats you knew you wanted to hit throughout the show: Pit Girl, the scientists, rescue. Anything you can’t wait for us to see, in broad terms?

NICKERSON I don’t think it’s a spoiler to say that them coming back to New Jersey has always been a huge thing we wanted to do, and, in some sense, is the show.

LYLE There are a few things. There’s a scene in episode five that we’ve been talking about for many seasons.

NICKERSON Oh yeah, that is going to be really good! We’ve been talking about for a really long time.

There have been more than one scene that made your actors unwell — and even had them throwing up. For example, the Jackie feast … the Pit Girl reveal. Was there any filming experience in this final season that’s comparable to that?

LYLE I think they toughened up a little bit.

NICKERSON I mean, eating Jackie was rough. That was a tough day!

LYLE That was really, really rough. I don’t know that we could ever top that, in terms of torturing our actors.

NICKERSON Because that thing [Jackie’s edible body] looked good. I mean, not tasty, but, oh man. Just to have what they were going to eat like around is tough.

LYLE There was a moment on set this season when Melanie [Lynskey] brought her daughter to set and sort of regretted it immediately. Like, “Oh, just kidding! Go into the trailer.” I was like, “That’s not real. It’s okay!” She seemed fine. I mean, we don’t have to pay for her therapy! (Laughs.)

Yellowjackets is now streaming the first episode of season four on Paramount+ Premium.

#710. Despite restrictive abortion laws, Poland's 'Abortomat' — a locker that dispenses abortion pills — helps women who want to end a pregnancy

Abortion laws in Poland are very restrictive. Activists there have found a new way to help women wanting to terminate a pregnancy: the "Abortomat," a locker that dispenses abortion pills. But they face fierce opposition.

Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.

Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.

In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

The "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.

Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.

"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.

Women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.

In 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.

Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.

Dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, said the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated."

She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.

"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she said.

The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," said Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.

At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan."

"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she said.

Earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.

Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.

"I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she said.

"I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.

In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.

Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

"I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she said.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.

In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.

The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.

Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents said they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.

Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

#709. How ‘I Play Rocky’ Star P.J. Byrne Became One of Hollywood’s Go-To Character Actors

The Scorsese favorite has shared scenes with Leonardo DiCaprio and Margot Robbie. Now he's playing Irwin Winkler, the producing legend behind 'Rocky' and 'Goodfellas.'

Ever since P.J. Byrne had a literal meltdown in the most showstopping scene of Damien Chazelle’s Babylon, his career as a scene-stealing character actor has reached a new high.

The New Jersey native’s 2026 alone has brought eight credits, including the conclusion of his recurring character on The Boys, Coyote vs. Acme, The End of Oak Street and a series-regular role on USA’s basic cable hit The Rainmaker. Most notably, he now stars in his biggest film role to date as Oscar-winning Rocky producer Irwin Winkler in Peter Farrelly’s biographical awards contender, I Play Rocky. Related Stories Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Feasting With $120M+ in Franchise's Box Office Comeback Hollywood Flashback Yo, Academy! When 'Rocky' Was Crowned Best Picture Champ

In 1975, Winkler and his producing partner Robert Chartoff were developing Martin Scorsese’s New York, New York at the same time as the underdog story from a then-unknown Sylvester Stallone. The former would become the first of a half-dozen films Winkler collaborated on with Scorsese, including 2013’s The Wolf of Wall Street. It’s fitting, then, that Byrne is now playing the celebrated producer, given that his own career turning point came with his role as Rugrat in Scorsese and Leonardo DiCaprio’s unhinged take on the life of former stockbroker Jordan Belfort. (Byrne would later reunite with Scorsese on his 2016 series Vinyl.)

Byrne’s turn as a founding member of Belfort’s Stratton Oakmont is probably best remembered for one particularly rambunctious trading-floor scene in which his character shaves a female sales assistant’s head. The opportunity also allowed Byrne to put his unused finance degree from Boston College to work, albeit in a fictionalized version of a career path he had quickly abandoned because of his aversion to boiler-room culture.

In the mid-’90s, one of his Boston College professors encouraged him to try his hand at drama school instead, leading him to DePaul University in Chicago. Byrne’s time in the Windy City seems to have left a lasting impression. He often speaks about acting in the same terms that Chicago Bulls legend Michael Jordan once used to describe his record-setting 3-point barrage against the Portland Trail Blazers in Game 1 of the 1992 NBA Finals. When Byrne acts, he strives to enter a flow state, or “the zone,” as Jordan called it, where he’s so locked in to the task at hand that distractions fade and he can achieve peak performance.

Byrne’s Wolf of Wall Street video audition featured a monologue he reimagined from the ground up. Channeling his brief experience in the financial world, he portrayed his stockbroker character emotionally manipulating a widow into forking over $100,000 during a sales call. Scorsese appreciated the creative risk so much that he recited part of the speech back to Byrne during their eventual in-person callback. Byrne’s improvisational instincts and willingness to take creative leaps through punch-ups and alternative dialogue are muscles he first developed during his early days in Los Angeles.

At the turn of the century, Byrne put himself through the wringer of commercial auditions. With a talent pool far deeper than most people might expect, he knew he needed to find a way to stand out. That meant arriving with his own variations on the material or improvising in the moment. To pay the bills between sporadic acting jobs, he provided script coverage and handled other development duties at the production company of family friend and fellow Boston College alum Chris O’Donnell.

Eventually, he left his VP position to focus solely on acting. Nameless parts soon gave way to small but named roles, though there were milestones along the way that reinforced his greater pursuit. One came when he made Will Ferrell and Stephen Colbert laugh during a table-read scene in Nora Ephron’s Bewitched (2005). Byrne played a TV writer in the film, an early example of the showbiz-affiliated roles that would become a calling card throughout his career. He speculates that his time working in development may have influenced that pattern.

Byrne’s road to I Play Rocky can also be traced back to commercials cast by casting director Rick Montgomery. It further involved producer Toby Emmerich’s tenure as head of New Line, during which Byrne made memorable appearances in the label’s Horrible Bosses and Final Destination 5. Above all, Byrne won a major fan in Farrelly when he played a record executive in the best picture-winning Green Book, followed by Dear Santa, the Christmas comedy Farrelly co-wrote for his brother Bobby to direct.

“After Green Book, Peter was like, ‘You need your Paul Giamatti [in Sideways] part. You need a bigger part in a movie,’” Byrne tells The Hollywood Reporter.

The role of Irwin Winkler still didn’t come easy. In the behind-the-scenes narrative, Winkler and Chartoff desperately want to produce Stallone’s Rocky screenplay, but he refuses to sell it unless he gets to star as the title character. Winkler and Chartoff, ever the pragmatists, try to give the aspiring young actor and screenwriter a reality check about how star power drives the financing and green-lighting of most movies. But Stallone stands his ground despite increasingly lucrative offers for the script.

Eventually, Winkler and Chartoff realize they shouldn’t be producing an underdog story about a small-time boxer named Rocky Balboa if they aren’t willing to practice what they preach. So they risk everything, including their names and their homes, to install Stallone as the star, all while distributor United Artists sets him up to fail at every turn in hopes of replacing him with a proven commodity.

The casting of Byrne’s role also became rather meta because the I Play Rocky brain trust initially sought a name for Winkler. With relative unknown Anthony Ippolito already cast as young Sly, it’s understandable why they would want to shore up the surrounding roles with established, butts-in-seats actors. But the producers of I Play Rocky ultimately arrived at the same conclusion as the producers of Rocky — gamble on talent, not status.

“They wanted to get a name, because there weren’t a lot of names [in this cast]. But they were also living in the world of, If we’re going to cast Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone, then let’s give other people shots too,” Byrne says. “They all knew me from these small parts. Then they just believed in me enough to give me a shot. I want to tell the world that there’s honestly no small parts. Someone will ultimately give you a chance.”

Below, in a conversation with THR, Byrne also discusses the day his improvisational skills resulted in I Play Rocky’s most hilarious scene. He also addresses whether the strained relationship between Winkler and Stallone in recent years influenced his take at all.

It’s not talent. I just have three children. I have to pay for their lives. That’s all that is. It’s like, Yes, I’ll do that. I have three children.

You’ve still cemented yourself as one of the industry’s go-to character actors.

I always say ABC: always be classy. So I don’t know if I can admit to that, but I do have repeat buyers, if you will, because they’re buddies. Once I work on anything, I tend to have repeat business. So I’ll meet you halfway. I hate giving myself flowers like that, but I believe in myself to deliver. And if other people see that, then I appreciate it.

When you hear labels like “character actor” or “comic relief” or “scene-stealer,” do you bristle at all? Or do you embrace the lane you’ve carved out for yourself?

It’s funny. I don’t even look at it that way. All ships rise with the tide. I want everyone to score and win. I’m always surrounded by incredible actors in everything I do, so everyone passes the ball nicely. It’s not about being funny or stealing scenes. It’s, How do I make these moments pop more? This sounds so cheesy and trite, but it’s really, How do I service the director or the writer? I’ve been doing this so long that they are often my really good friends.

When someone makes a movie, they’ve put four years of their life into it. They’ve battled producers and studio executives to get this one day of this particular scene, and half their budget is being spent on a goddamn crane shot. So I just want to do everything I can for them. I put in the work, and my brain just naturally looks for moments that can pop. Is there an ability to make this zeitgeisty so that people can relate to it and it can become its own thing?

I started out in Los Angeles doing commercials, and I was baptized by fire doing them. Commercials are like street basketball. It’s rough. They’re not nice to you. The rooms aren’t sweet. They’re not kind. But some of the best actors are commercial actors. They just never found the right lane or the right agent. They’re still out there, and they’re extraordinary actors. But adding jokes during commercial auditions is how I trained my brain to find moments to pop. I would think of the fifth funniest joke in my brain because the first four would probably be thought of by someone else.

That mindset succeeds in scenarios where I have fearless directors who’ve proven themselves. It’s usually the great directors like Marty Scorsese or Peter Farrelly or Damien Chazelle who don’t have to worry about notes from everyone. They know I’ve done the work and have their vision in mind, so they’ll take the handcuffs off me. They’ll be like, “Just add stuff. We trust you. Go.” They know that before a job, I’ll literally sit in a hotel room for two weeks and have food sent up while I make sure I’m doing everything I can for them. I don’t want to let anyone down.

You’re also asked to play showbiz people fairly often. The Boys, Babylon, The Big Cigar and A Complete Unknown are only a few examples, as is your current role as Irwin Winkler in I Play Rocky. Do you have any theories why this has become your niche?

I feel like I have a face like that. I also do a lot of period pieces and play a lot of lawyers. That’s just what’s filming now. But I think it’s all because I know those characters well from when I started out in Los Angeles.

I owe a lot to Chris O’Donnell. When he was Robin [in Batman & Robin], he had a production company at Warner Bros. His sisters and my sister are really good friends. And because I had a finance degree from Boston College, I was like, If acting doesn’t work out, I can be an intern with them. To his credit, his company gave me a script and were like, “Hey, do coverage on this script.” So I did, and the coverage was called “brilliant.” But it was only brilliant because I literally just went to grad school where I learned arc and character. I literally just wrote papers for three years.

Chris was like, “Be our story editor.” And I was like, “Chris, I came here to act.” Then he gave me the greatest gift ever when he said, “No, come and go as you please.” So I was able to walk onto the Warner Bros. and work for him, while also doing commercials and small TV jobs. Every time I tried to quit, they were like, “You’re a vice president right now.”

I set up movies. I learned the business. I would walk past The West Wing and ER stages, and I told myself that I wouldn’t set foot on those stages until I was invited. And I did eventually book those jobs. So I became comfortable being in that environment, and it wasn’t so daunting going into those rooms.

It’s because of all those early experiences that I have a lot of friends who are producers, writers and directors. So I know this world well, and when someone says, “Play this showbiz part,” I’m like, “Trust me, I got it.”

You worked with Peter Farrelly on Green Book and Dear Santa. Did he go straight to you for Irwin Winkler?

It wasn’t straight to me, but I love Peter forever. I want to tell the world that there’s honestly no small parts, and you never know what’s going to come around. And that’s why this movie was so super meta for me. They wanted to get a name, because there weren’t a lot of names [in this cast]. But they were also living in the world of, If we’re going to cast Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone, then let’s give other people shots too.

After Green Book, Peter was like, “You need your Paul Giamatti [in Sideways] part. You need a bigger part in a movie.” [I Play Rocky casting director] Rick Montgomery cast me in commercials years ago, and [producer] Toby Emmerich also ran New Line when I had small parts in Horrible Bosses and Final Destination 5.

So they all knew me from these small parts, and they all said, “He’s ready to have a bigger part. Come audition for this.” Then they just believed in me enough to give me a shot. Someone will ultimately give you a chance, just like they once gave it to Sylvester Stallone and now Anthony Ippolito and me.

Everything is driven by the same dozen names now, so it’s nice to hear that Farrelly is looking elsewhere.

Yeah, he’s incredibly loyal. If you look at his movies, the same people always come back. When you go out for drinks with Pete, 32 people show up with him. I love that idea of a family. Working with friends is the best way to go to work, and that’s another reason why I get repeat business.

When it’s four in the morning on a Friday night and you’ve been shooting 12 hours, we’re still cheerleaders for each other. I love those kinds of sets. It kills me when I see people being cancers or want to get off set. Again, I know what my friend went through to be here after four years. So I always say, “Let’s deliver this moment the best way we can because we’re never coming back.”

What went through your mind when you first witnessed Anthony Ippolito’s take on Sly?

It was at a table read, and while everybody does a version of Sylvester Stallone, I was like, We’re living and dying on this kid. This is the moment. And as soon as he opened his mouth, it was so subtle and soulful and full of heart. It honestly surpassed what my expectation was going to be. I have been doing this a long time, and this is the biggest part I’ve ever gotten in a movie. It’s so beautiful for me, personally. But I can’t help but get so psyched for this kid because he’s so spectacular.

I’ve been around some incredible performances. I watched Leo just destroy on The Wolf of Wall Street. And Margot Robbie, I still wish she got her flowers for Babylon. There’s even a scene with me and Laura Dern on Big Little Lies. When you’re an actor in a scene with them and the camera’s not on you, there’s just a moment when you become an audience member. And you’re like, Oh shit, it’s happening. You can feel it in the room and you want to deliver for them and be there for them. And that’s what happened with Anthony.

He was in the zone. That’s what basketball players say when the net looks like the size of an ocean and they can’t miss. That’s what it felt like watching Anthony. He was so good that I kept thinking, Did Sylvester Stallone travel through space and time to possess this kid’s body? That’s how special it was. Then Pete would call cut, and Anthony would come back online and say, “Hey, what are we getting for dinner tonight?” And I was just like, “What is going on right now?” Peter and I were like, “Is he the world’s greatest actor?” He also played Rocky and Sylvester Stallone, and it was just crazy to watch him play two different characters.

I also watched Timothée Chalamet be Bob Dylan, and that was another time where I was like, “Holy shit.” But Timmy would stay in character, unlike Anthony. So everyone has their own method, and there is no right way.

There’s no love lost between Stallone and Winkler in recent years. Sly resents the fact that Winkler retains full ownership of the Rocky franchise and that he doesn’t have a piece of the pie to leave for his family. Did you and Farrelly ever discuss planting that seed of acrimony for where their relationship would end up?

Producers are observers. They are there to eliminate risk, put out fires and make sure that the art happens. Sometimes, they have to guide it and have their influence, but that’s what they are. Bob Chartoff and Irwin Winkler were the greatest producers and the ultimate backstop to any ball getting past the catcher. So that’s what I had to deal with in my role.

The first time you meet my character, he’s all business. He’s not mean to Sly, but he just doesn’t look the part for the role being cast. But then he’s intrigued by this smart guy sitting in front of him, and then they eventually read his scripts to see that there’s talent there. At first, Winkler believes in the project, and then he learns to believe in the person behind it.

The end of the movie shows the real-life clip of when Rocky won best picture at the 1977 Oscars. Bob Chartoff and Irwin Winkler stood up, and Irwin Winkler immediately grabbed Sylvester Stallone to join them on stage, which is rare. It’s usually just the producers who accept the best picture award.

But Winkler grabbed Sylvester Stallone and put his arm around him with such love. It was like, This is my son. I believe in you so much. I mortgaged my house for you. I didn’t just bet on a movie. I bet on a child that I love. It’s the idea that you would do anything for your kids, and like I said, I literally work for my children. The money comes in the door, and it goes right to give them every opportunity to succeed in life.

Whatever the extraneous stuff is between them now, I was meant to portray that period of time in the late ‘70s. I was there to share the message that if you really fucking do the work and you believe in yourself — and then you surround yourself with like-minded people who truly believe in you as well — then anything is possible. Maybe you too will one day win an Oscar. That was a special moment in all of their lives, and that’s what I needed to play and had to play.

In a perfect world, a clause would kick in after x amount of years so that the original creator receives at least a sliver of the pie. But like you said, Winkler and Chartoff risked their homes on a complete unknown. They also gave him profit participation on the first film, as well as most, if not all, of the future films. So I hate to both-sides the issue, but I really do see both sides here.

Of course, I thought about all of that and who these people are today and yesterday. But my job was to play that moment in time in which greatness happened. It was a beautiful thing, even if you’re always battling for what you want and going at it. That’s why I have that moment after Winkler found out that Sly and Carl Weathers had never boxed before.

Yeah, Winkler went out and got the world’s greatest boxing choreographer, but then Sly kicked him out. All the script had was Winkler saying, “It’s a boxing movie!” So I said to Peter, “The producer’s job is to put out fires, so he would lose his mind right now. This is a handcuffs-off moment. Let me riff and play a little bit here.” It was a scary moment because it was late at night right before Thanksgiving, and everybody wanted to go home for Thanksgiving. But here I was adding a lot to the scene.

To Peter’s credit, he let me go. I made that line up about The Godfather: “It’s not about the mafia. It’s about a nice Italian family that loves pasta.” Then, because he’s angry, he has to get the fuck out of the room. So I went up the stairs toward the door, and I added the lines about how this “happens to be” a set of stairs and how this “happens to be” a door as he walks out. So you do go at it when you’re making films because you’re passionate about the product.

Yeah, the “happens to be” scene is your “hello, college!” scene of this movie. Winkler’s meltdown is rooted in director John G. Avildsen’s position that Rocky isn’t a boxing movie. He made the point that it’s a character study about a guy who “happens to be” a boxer. Plus, it hits close to home because every entertainment journalist has written some version of that “happens to be” line about a story in which the surrounding world is incidental.

Those improvised lines came from being in the zone. It’s the best when it happens. I also didn’t know that guy was going to ask me to take off his jacket. We were just playing in the moment. They let this little chemistry experiment happen.

The Rocky and Apollo fight is ultimately saved for the closing credits, serving as the punchline to the “happens to be” bit. I Play Rocky is also a character study that happens to have boxing in it.

Was that fight always intended for the credits? Or did they realize in the edit that it would make for a great gag?

It had another great ending as well. Rocky was boxing, and when they called cut, he didn’t want to hear it. Then he was like, “I can go again.” He’d been going and going for 28 days, and then his wife came up to say, “It’s over.” And he was like, “No, no, I can do one more.”And she was like, “No, it’s over. You did it.” I could cry right now just thinking about how they ended it.

But Anthony’s earlier moment where he was hitting the door as Rocky and going, “It stinks! My life stinks!” — how were we going to top how extraordinary that was? We couldn’t top that. Showing it toward the end also has a beautiful message, so that’s moviemaking. You’re learning and adapting and changing as you’re going.

Peter also edits as he’s going, and he knows the movie so well. Like Avildsen in the movie, I would add something, and Peter would be like, “We got it. Cut. Moving on.” And I’d be like, “What do you mean you got it? I only said the line once.” And he was like, “No, no, it’s great.” This is the first movie I saw six weeks after filming it, so I remembered every second of filming. And when some of those moments came up, I was like, He was right. That is great. We didn’t need another angle.

If you had to guess, how much of Rocky did Farrelly recreate?

Oh God, if I was going to throw out a number, maybe 26.9 percent. I don’t know. They shot that boxing scene for a week, and that was the longest, most expensive part of the shoot.

I wish I could’ve seen Amazon’s response to it ending up in the closing credits.

(Laughs.) Again, to Peter’s credit, he said, “What do we think the best part of the story is?” That’s an amazing thing. The great directors are fearless. They don’t operate from fear. They trust their instincts and their gut. They have great editors too.

Some locations probably don’t exist in the same form anymore, but for places like Rocky’s apartment, did you revisit as many original spots as possible from Rocky?

We shot at the same apartment he lived in, and it’s still a rough neighborhood to this day. We heard people around the neighborhood say, “Oh my God, this feels just like yesterday.” Some of the same people lived there 50 years ago.

Then we went to the Rocky Steps [at the Philadelphia Museum of Art], which was amazing. AnnaSophia Robb and I ran up the stairs with Anthony. Then I came back down the stairs, and Tracy Letts was there, so I have the greatest video of me and Tracy Letts running up the stairs together. I have to post it. It’s so beautiful that all these people come from around the world to run up the stairs in their gray sweatsuits. I have another little video of Anthony waiting in line to take a picture next to the statue of Rocky, dressed as Rocky.

So it was really special to be in Philadelphia. It’s a super-duper city, man. You feel the lunch-pale vibe. We all knew how special this movie is to so many people around the world, and while Sylvester, Irwin Winkler and SteadiCam creator Garrett Brown are still alive, we didn’t want to let them down. We truly felt that way.

Overall, the movie is largely about the power of no. Sly said no to Winkler and Chartoff countless times before he got the deal he thought he wanted at the time. Have you had a chance to say no to something that ultimately proved to be the best decision?

My whole life is built on not understanding what the word no means. I was supposed to work on Wall Street, but then I decided to walk away to be an actor. I was told, “You can’t be an actor,” and I was like, “Yes, I can.”

To me, no just means not now, and my whole life is built on that premise. Nothing is impossible. That’s why I love the movie business, and that’s what made Irwin and Bob incredible producers. They didn’t understand the word no either. If something went wrong on a film, they fixed it.

Marty Scorsese talks about this all the time [from his experiences with Winkler]. He says, “All this craziness was happening in the background, and Irwin Winkler never let me know any of it. I was just there to be free and think about the project.” So I wanted to put a little of that into I Play Rocky [when Winkler and Chartoff opt not to tell Sly they’ve mortgaged their homes to keep the movie going].

I’ve always loved movies and shows about the making of famous movies or shows. Of all your other projects, is there one that would make for a compelling behind-the-scenes narrative à la I Play Rocky?

Oh, it’d be Coyote vs. Acme. My dear friend, Dave Green, directed it, and the world almost never saw it. It was going to be thrown in a vault because an accountant made a decision. We should always be art over commerce, especially when you’ve chosen to make movies for a living. I had a front row seat to what Dave went through, and he was so classy through the whole process.

Another heartbreaking aspect to the story is that [Looney Tunes character voice actor] Eric Bauza just passed away. It’s a bummer. He was a generational talent, and he was also one of the classiest, nicest guys you’ve ever met. It just kills me. He has an eight-year-old kid and a fiancée. He literally stood up for the movie while presenting at an award show and said, “Release Coyote vs. Acme!” He said that to the corporation that paid him all his money and fed him because he voiced Looney Tunes characters.

On set, it was amazing what we did because we had no money. I wasn’t even playing that part [of Acme lawyer, Bill Pelicanos] the week before. They were like, “John Cena is going to do it. Do you want to be a sidekick?” And I was like, “Yes! I want my hair to look exactly like his, and I also want to be bald in a scene.” And they were like, “We can’t afford any of that.” And I was like, “I’m calling in favors for hair.” Everyone was doing favors for everybody on that movie. We believed in the art.

It was so meta because it was about fighting big corporations. Everyone was doing that movie for the right reason. So that would truly make for a special behind-the-scenes movie. I also just found out it can get nominated for best animated feature because over 75 percent of the project is animated. I really hope it gets its flowers.

If Babylon got the I Play Rocky treatment, what would the behind the scenes of the “hello, college!” sequence look like?

Well, we shot that 10-minute scene over three days. It was one of the greatest, most fun shooting experiences of my life because, once again, Damien let me go. I auditioned during COVID, when you couldn’t be in the room together, and I got a note back from Damien saying, “It feels like you want to really let it go.” At first, I was like, I want to stay close to the lines because this is Damien Chazelle. I’ve never auditioned for him. I love this dude. I want to be in his movie so badly.

But once he said, “Go,” I added so many horrible things. Then I handed it in, and 20 minutes later, I got the call that I got the part. When I showed up on set, I saw that the lines I had added were in the movie, and that’s when I knew I was going to riff even more. Damien ended up letting everybody play.

My close-ups were on the last day, and I had basically already lost my voice. It ended up being gone for a month. But something came out of me that day to make it all happen. When I did the first take of my close-up, they were like, “Great. That was amazing. We got it.” But I was like, “Let’s keep going. I have four more ideas. I’m going to lose my voice. I want to get it all.” We still had a game left to play, and I didn’t want to celebrate yet.

Everybody knew how special and spectacular that scene was, and everyone was cheering for everybody when it was their take. Those special days also had moments in the zone. I was able to be conscious of how amazing this was and still deliver new stuff.

Did they actually keep the stage extra warm given the nature of the scene?

I mean, it was hot, but that was mostly just incredible makeup. They put this gel on your head that looks like sweat. Those were three days of magic, man. Damien had a big board of all the shots he wanted, and we just checked them off as we went. It was awesome.

What about The Wolf of Wall Street? How would you dramatize one of those days?

That was an amazing brotherhood. I’m still friends with so many of those guys. Jon Bernthal lived across the hall from me. Kenny Choi lived downstairs. Brian Sacca and Ethan Suplee were also close, and we had a blast. We knew how powerful that story was.

Leo sometimes likes to stay in character, but he joked, “If I stayed in character this whole time, I would have a nervous breakdown.” So we got the real Leo. We got to bro out with a buddy. He’s the man of our times. He’s the great actor. He’s charming. He’s the best storyteller. He wanted us all to have a great time. He was also producing, so he made sure that we met the real Jordan Belfort and learned how to sell from the guy. The idea was that we needed to really see who this guy is and how these people truly operate.

As I mentioned earlier, the greatness of Marty is that he let us all riff and play. So I riffed with Jonah [Hill] and Leo, and that was another magical experience because I probably made up 80 percent of the lines I said in that movie. Marty was always like, “It’s too clean. Mess it up. Go.”

When I auditioned, I used my finance degree to make up my own monologue, and Marty knew it. So he memorized it and read it back to me. I was like, This is the greatest day of my life. Then, on the first day of rehearsal, Marty and Leo asked me questions about finance. I was like, I can’t believe I’m sitting here answering their finance questions. This is crazy. Am I an actor? Am I a consultant? What is happening?

Years from now, when you write your memoir, how will you sum up the 2026 chapter?

“He was the hardest working person on the set, and he was always classy.” The title of the biography should be P.J. Byrne: Over the Shoulder and Out of Focus.

***I Play Rocky is now playing in movie theaters nationwide.

#708. Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.

The findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an important role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.

The discovery could be especially important for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.

Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression

To investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.

As researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.

Participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.

"Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy said. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes."

One possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.

Rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially important, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.

When these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.

"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy said.

Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.

Even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.

Someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.

Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.

"As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy said. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake."

A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits

The research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains important, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.

Because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.

Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.

For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.

The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.

Materials provided by University of Missouri-Columbia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

A new supernova has been spotted exploding in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433, about 50 million light-years from Earth.

Researchers have discovered a new supernova called SN 2026ahvu. A Type Ia supernova, this event took place in a system with two stars orbiting one another (also known as a binary system), in which typically one star is an exploding white dwarf.

During most type Ia supernovae, the white dwarf pulls material away from the other star until enough accumulates on its surface to create an explosion.

Finding galaxies where stellar explosions are taking place isn't a rarity. However, this supernova is unique in how early it was captured. If the supernova were starting to dim, researchers might infer that the event was ending. However, according to details shared when it was first spotted, as well as later observations, this supernova was discovered while getting brighter.

This indicates that the supernova was likely caught early in the process of exploding, providing researchers with a unique opportunity to observe the event as it is taking place. By exploring observations of the galaxy before, during and (in the future) after the supernova event, researchers can investigate this type Ia supernova and how it affected the system in which it took place.

Scientists made this discovery using ATLAS, or the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact System, which is a robotic astronomical survey made up of telescopes across both hemispheres.

ATLAS is designed to spot incoming near-Earth objects like asteroids before they can reach Earth. It's essentially an asteroid impact early warning system.

But just because that's what the system is designed for doesn't mean that's all it can do. The system can also spot other objects moving through space and, in this instance, it was able to capture observations of this supernova.

Following its initial discovery, other observations of the supernova were made using NOIRLab's Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and Gemini South telescope.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. #706. Bassam Tariq Says Marvel’s Scrapped ‘Blade’ Reboot Taught Him “Life’s Too Short to Make Sh** Films”

"It was funny and strange to start casting and building without a proper script... That's also very dangerous because if the text comes and it doesn't add up to what you were saying, your credibility gets completely shot," the director said in a new interview.

Bassam Tariq is opening up about what he learned working on Marvel‘s scrapped Blade reboot.

In an interview with The New Arab published Friday, the Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother director was asked what his time working in the “studio system” taught him about how he wants to approach filmmaking. Tariq said it felt “dangerous” to begin casting without “a proper script,” and that he prefers to “have full control over my script.”

“It was funny and strange to start casting and building without a proper script. You’re sitting there and explaining to actors what their role will be, and they just have to believe you,” he said. “That’s also very dangerous because if the text comes and it doesn’t add up to what you were saying, your credibility gets completely shot. All I have is my integrity, and I’ve been thinking about that a lot.” Related Stories Hollywood Flashback When Kevin Feige Got Off to a Less-Than-Incredible Start at Marvel TV 'VisionQuest' Creator Terry Matalas Tells All About That Supersized Finale and Post-Credits Surprise

In 2021, it was reported that Tariq was attached to helm Marvel’s Blade film; Mahershala Ali was announced as the project’s star seven years ago at Comic-Con 2019. The actor confirmed in a July interview with GQ that he would not be leading Blade.

The Hollywood Reporter exclusively reported in September 2022 that Tariq had exited the project, with the director saying in a statement at the time, “It’s been an honor working with the wonderful folks at Marvel. We were able to put together a killer cast and crew. Eager to see where the next director takes the film.”

Tariq continued in his interview with The New Arab, “If you’re the bearer of bad news to your actors, but you’re not the one making any of these decisions — and it’s actually coming from a corporate entity — that’s not a great way to be a director. I know some people can take that and run with it, but I learned I was losing credibility with my actors, and it wasn’t a healthy way to operate as a filmmaker.”

In short, the director said his “big lesson” was that he wanted to have full control of the scripts of his films, noting “life’s too short to make shit films.” Tariq added, “If we disagree, it’s between them and me. It’s quite sad because we had such high hopes for what we wanted to build.”

Ali said in a September interview with GQ that he agrees the failed film is Kevin Feige’s “biggest failure.”

When asked why the film didn’t happen with the interviewer, the Oscar winner said, “That’s a Kevin Feige question.” He continued, “They had, as you said, a two-time Oscar-winning actor under contract and you got billions of dollars. That’s a question for them. I don’t mean anything personal to you, but I don’t know why it didn’t. To this day, I don’t know why it didn’t happen. I just know that it was — Kevin, he said it was the biggest failure of his career and I agree.”

#705. A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections

A common amino acid found in everyday foods could play a surprisingly important role in helping the immune system recognize cancer and fight viral infections. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that when the body runs low on arginine, a key part of its immune defense system can stop working properly, potentially allowing dangerous cells and viruses to escape detection.

Arginine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally and also obtains from protein-rich foods. It is essential for making proteins that perform countless functions throughout the body. Researchers have long known that unusually low arginine levels are associated with several diseases, including colon cancer, but exactly how this shortage affects the body's defenses has remained unclear.

Now, new research suggests that restoring arginine levels could help the immune system respond more effectively to serious threats. In experiments involving mice, increasing dietary arginine reduced the formation of colon cancer tumors and lessened the severity of influenza and SARS-CoV-2 infections. Remarkably, providing arginine after mice had already contracted influenza also improved their outcomes.

The findings, published in the journal Cell, raise the possibility that an inexpensive, readily available supplement could eventually become a useful addition to cancer treatments and strategies for combating viral infections. However, further research in humans is needed to determine whether the benefits observed in mice translate into effective treatments for people.

How a Missing Nutrient Could Help Cancer Escape the Immune System

The research was led by Sohail Tavazoie, who directs the Elizabeth and Vincent Meyer Laboratory of Systems Cancer Biology at Rockefeller University. His team has spent years investigating how arginine influences cancer development and progression.

In 2023, the researchers discovered that depriving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more genetic mutations. These changes can contribute to the unpredictable behavior of cancer cells, raising important questions about how arginine shortages might influence the disease.

The latest study reveals another potentially significant consequence. When arginine becomes scarce, cells struggle to produce enough of a crucial immune system protein known as MHC-1. This protein acts as a warning system, helping immune cells identify potential dangers such as cancerous changes or viral infections.

Without enough MHC-1, abnormal or infected cells may become harder for the immune system to recognize.

Encouragingly, the researchers also found that supplying a moderate amount of arginine, comparable to the quantity available in a couple of over-the-counter supplement tablets, could help restore production of this important protein.

"Our work reveals how a lack of arginine interferes with the immune system, and suggests that upping arginine intake could prove beneficial," says first author Qiushuang Wu, a postdoc in the lab. "Perhaps that means it could be used in combination with other therapies to treat both cancer and viral infections."

"Arginine supplementation could be readily tested in patients receiving immunotherapies or given to high-risk populations exposed to viral pathogens," Tavazoie suggests. "Considering that arginine is inexpensive and readily available, we hope that therapeutic and preventative studies could be undertaken soon."

The Surprising Connection Between Arginine and Immune Defenses

To understand why arginine has such an important effect, the researchers investigated how cells use amino acids to manufacture proteins.

Proteins are built from amino acids according to genetic instructions encoded in DNA. These instructions are copied into messenger RNA, which carries the information to the cellular machinery responsible for protein production.

The instructions are read in groups of three genetic letters called codons. Each codon specifies an amino acid or provides another signal needed during protein production. Arginine is unusual in that six different codons can specify it, reflecting the multiple ways its incorporation into proteins can be encoded.

Scientists already knew that changes in amino acid availability could affect cellular metabolism and signaling, two processes that help regulate how cells obtain energy and respond to their surroundings. What remained less clear was whether shortages of particular amino acids could directly influence which proteins cells produce.

To investigate, Wu examined the effects of arginine availability across several disease models, including colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2. Each of these diseases has previously been associated with abnormal levels of various amino acids.

The research was supported in part by the Stavros Niarchos Foundation (SNF) Institute for Global Infectious Disease Research at The Rockefeller University and the Weill Cancer East Hub.

"One of the most dramatic patterns to emerge was that arginine was the most depleted amino acid in all of these diseases," she says.

Why Low Arginine Levels Can Disrupt the Immune System

In laboratory experiments using cultured cells, Wu examined how arginine shortages affected protein production. She identified 414 proteins whose levels dropped abnormally when arginine was scarce.

Many of these proteins were associated with biological functions already known to depend on arginine. However, the researchers uncovered a more unexpected effect involving three genes from the HLA family.

These genes provide instructions for producing proteins associated with MHC-I (major histocompatibility complex class I), an essential component of the immune system's ability to recognize threats.

MHC-I proteins are displayed on the surfaces of cells throughout the body. They act somewhat like identification displays, presenting small fragments of proteins from inside the cell to immune cells known as T cells.

When these displays reveal suspicious material, such as proteins produced by a virus or abnormal proteins associated with cancer, T cells can recognize the danger and help coordinate an immune response.

But the researchers found that arginine deficiency interfered with the production of these molecular warning signals.

The reason involved ribosomes, the tiny cellular machines that assemble proteins by following genetic instructions. Because the proteins involved in MHC-I production require arginine at numerous points, the researchers suspected that an insufficient supply could interfere with their assembly.

Further experiments confirmed that suspicion. When arginine was unavailable, ribosomes stalled while trying to manufacture MHC-I proteins. Without enough of the required amino acid, the cells could not efficiently complete the process.

As a result, fewer MHC-I proteins reached the cell surface, reducing the signals that would normally alert T cells to cancer-associated or viral proteins. This created an opportunity for dangerous cells to avoid immune detection.

"These findings are exciting because they reveal that consumption of a specific amino acid can directly regulate gene expression in an organism by increasing production of a protein enriched in that amino acid," Tavazoie says. "We believe that such selective translational tuning of gene expression through dietary manipulation likely extends to many other proteins and amino acids."

More Arginine Meant Fewer Colon Cancer Tumors in Mice

After identifying the molecular mechanism, Wu investigated whether changing the amount of arginine in an animal's diet could influence disease outcomes.

Mice receiving diets low in arginine developed more colon cancer tumors. In contrast, mice consuming higher amounts of the amino acid developed fewer tumors.

These findings provided evidence that arginine availability can influence cancer development through its effects on the immune system, rather than simply changing how individual cancer cells behave.

The results also raised a broader question: If arginine helps immune cells recognize cancer, could it provide similar benefits when the body encounters dangerous viruses?

Arginine Also Improved Outcomes From Influenza and COVID-19 Viruses

To explore that possibility, Wu collaborated with Heinz-Heinrich Hoffman, a research assistant professor in Charles Rice's Laboratory of Virology and Infectious Disease.

Together, they examined the effects of dietary arginine in mouse models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

The findings followed the same general pattern seen in the colon cancer experiments. Mice consuming more arginine experienced less severe symptoms from viral infections, suggesting that adequate levels of the amino acid helped support the body's immune defenses.

The researchers then made an even more surprising discovery.

Arginine did not appear to be beneficial only when consumed before an infection. Giving mice additional arginine after they had already been infected with influenza also improved their outcomes.

"Not only did mice with an arginine-rich diet have milder symptoms from viral infections, giving the mice arginine after influenza infection improved their outcomes too," Wu notes. "That was very surprising. From our genetic models, we knew manipulating arginine levels had a strong effect on gene expression, but we didn't expect the dietary manipulation to be equally impactful."

The observation suggests that changing nutrient availability might influence how the immune system responds even after a viral infection has taken hold.

Could a Simple Supplement Improve Cancer and Virus Treatments?

The discovery has potentially important implications for understanding why some people become more vulnerable to cancer and severe viral infections.

Arginine levels naturally decline with age, and inadequate nutrition can further reduce the amount available to cells. The researchers suspect that these changes may contribute to the weakening of immune defenses seen in certain diseases and in older adults.

"Qiushuang's findings illuminate how poor diet and aging -- during which arginine levels naturally decline -- could create the perfect storm for the initiation of colon cancer. Similarly, age-related arginine loss could partially contribute to the greater mortality caused by respiratory viruses," Tavazoie says. "We're also investigating whether making dietary changes in other amino acids has beneficial effects in a variety of disease contexts. There are no doubt more discoveries to come."

The possibility of using arginine alongside existing cancer immunotherapies is particularly intriguing. These treatments work by helping the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. If low arginine levels interfere with the molecular signals required for that recognition, restoring the nutrient might help some treatments work more effectively.

The researchers also see potential for investigating arginine supplementation in people at elevated risk of respiratory viral infections.

For now, these possibilities remain experimental. The findings do not establish that taking arginine supplements prevents or treats cancer, influenza, or COVID-19 in humans.

Nevertheless, the research reveals an important connection between nutrition and immunity. Rather than simply providing the raw materials needed to build proteins, specific amino acids may help determine how effectively the body's immune defenses identify and respond to dangerous threats.

And because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the discovery could provide a practical starting point for future studies aimed at strengthening the immune system against cancer and infectious diseases.

Fist my bump, everyone, because box office smash hit "Project Hail Mary" is heading back to theaters this December.

The exceptional sci-fi movie, based on Andy Weir's book, stars Ryan Gosling as Ryland Grace, a middle-school science teacher who becomes key to saving the world. Together with Rocky, an alien he meets along the way, Grace must solve the riddle of the mysterious substance that's causing the sun (and Rocky's star) to die out.

Amazon MGM has revealed the return to theaters with a video showcasing the many accolades that the film received. "Project Hail Mary" returns to the big screen on Dec. 11 and will be shown in all formats, including IMAX and 70MM.

"Project Hail Mary" was a massive success for Amazon MGM, grossing over $600 million worldwide when it first dropped in theaters back in March 2026. It was also a huge hit with critics, scoring an average of 95% on Rotten Tomatoes, and more importantly, getting two big thumbs up in our review!

Dec. 11 is a smart choice by MGM too, as it puts the sci-fi spectacle back in front of audiences a week ahead of Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part 3. That's not a battle you want to get in the middle of.

If you missed "Project Hail Mary" in theaters the first time, I'd definitely recommend you try to catch one of these screenings. It's a beautiful movie — visually and emotionally — and it deserves to be seen on the big screen.

If you're not feeling up to a trip to the theaters, you can also catch "Project Hail Mary" from the comfort of your own home, as it's also streaming on Amazon Prime Video.
