#675. Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom

Researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have accomplished something that physicists previously thought should not be possible. Using radio waves, they managed to directly control the magnetic spin of the nucleus inside a single atom. The unexpected result challenges existing assumptions about how atomic magnetism behaves and could eventually lead to new ways of storing and retrieving quantum information.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, also present scientists with a new puzzle. Although the experiment demonstrated that this remarkable level of control is possible, researchers do not yet fully understand the mechanism that makes it work.

Atoms in magnetic metals such as iron and nickel behave like tiny magnets. However, the magnetism within an atom comes from different sources. Both electrons and, in some cases, the atomic nucleus possess a quantum property called spin, which can be thought of as a miniature magnetic compass needle.

"By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons," says lead researcher Sander Otte. "But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world."

That protection makes nuclear spin especially interesting to quantum researchers. Because it is less exposed to disturbances from its surroundings, it could offer a promising way to preserve delicate quantum information.

To investigate these tiny magnetic properties, Otte's team uses a specially modified scanning tunneling microscope. This powerful instrument allows the researchers to deliver electrical signals to individual atoms with extraordinary precision.

Until recently, their experiments concentrated primarily on electron spin because it is easier to detect and measure. The nucleus's magnetic spin could only be observed indirectly through a phenomenon known as the hyperfine interaction, which creates a subtle quantum connection between the spins of the electron and nucleus. This connection can cause the two spins to become slightly entangled, meaning their quantum states are linked.

An Atomic Experiment Produces an Unexpected Result

In the latest study, lead author Hester Vennema and her colleagues took a different approach. They simultaneously applied two separate signals to a single atom, with one directed at the electron and the other at the nucleus.

By using these signals together, the researchers could investigate their effects independently. What happened next caught them by surprise.

Even when the electron and nuclear spins were largely disentangled, the team was still able to flip the orientation of the nucleus's magnetic spin. Based on their previous understanding, the nucleus should not have responded in this way.

"According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen," says Otte. "The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope."

The result suggests that the interaction between electrical signals and nuclear spin involves a mechanism that scientists have yet to fully explain.

Controlling Quantum Spins Like Guitar Strings

Achieving this level of precision required the researchers to adapt a technique called double magnetic resonance so it could operate on a single atom. The method allowed them to manipulate the magnetic behavior of the atomic nucleus separately from that of an electron.

Magnetic resonance works by applying a wave signal at a carefully selected frequency to change the orientation of a magnetic spin. However, quantum mechanics restricts these changes to specific allowed transitions, meaning the frequency must be precisely matched to the spin being targeted.

Vennema compares the process to playing a musical instrument.

"You can compare it to the strings of a guitar," Vennema explains. "Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The "notes" of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin."

In other words, electrons and atomic nuclei respond to very different frequencies, much as different guitar strings produce different musical notes. By tuning their signals to the appropriate frequencies, the scientists could address the two types of spin separately.

A Quantum Breakthrough With a Mystery Still to Solve

The discovery could have important implications for the future of quantum information technology. Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum systems can use quantum states to encode information in more complex ways.

One major challenge is keeping those states stable long enough for information to be stored and retrieved reliably. Nuclear spins are attractive candidates for quantum memory because they are relatively well isolated from environmental interference.

The ability to control these spins directly could therefore open new possibilities for writing, storing, and reading quantum information. However, the findings represent an early experimental advance rather than a ready-to-use quantum memory technology.

For now, one of the most important outcomes is the new scientific mystery the experiment has revealed. The researchers have demonstrated an unexpected way to manipulate nuclear spin, but the physical mechanism responsible remains unclear.

"Back to the drawing board, then," says Otte. "That is really how science works. There is always something new left to figure out."

#674. Box Office: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $56 Million on Friday, ‘I Play Rocky’ Follows With $3.8 Million

The odds were ever in the favor of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,” the latest entry in the storied franchise, which ruled the box office on Friday.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” generated $56 million from 4,018 North American theaters on Friday, taking the No. 1 spot on its opening day. It’s a strong start for the prequel, which looks to pull in around $120 million by Sunday. (That number far exceeds the cautious $85 million start the studio had projected.) Related Stories YouTube Refuses U.K. Government Request to Remove Russell Brand Video, Says It Is Investigating Content Emma Chamberlain, Wesley Wang, Aryna Sabalenka and More Unveil New Projects for YouTube

The Francis Lawrence-directed film takes place 25 years before the original “Hunger Games” series and follows the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy as he’s forced to compete in the second Quarter Quell. Joseph Zada, McKenna Grace, Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Elle Fanning and more star, with appearances from original “The Hunger Games” cast members Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Woodey Harleson.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” is the second prequel in the series, following 2023’s “The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes,” which finished its theatrical run at $363 million globally, making it a commercial success against a $100 million budget. With the new release, the “Hunger Games” franchise has generated more than $3.437 billion at the worldwide box office.

Amazon MGM’s “I Play Rocky” landed in second place on Friday, grossing $3.8 million from 2477 North American theaters following its wide expansion. The film is expected to gross $9.3 million by Sunday, bringing its cumulative total to $10.419 million. “I Play Rocky” previously brought in just under $1 million after two weekends in limited release.

The biopic-type film tells the true story behind the tumultuous making of the 1976 boxing classic “Rocky.” Anthony Ippolito portrays a young Sylvester Stallone, with AnnaSophia Robb, Kiki Seto, Matt Dillon, Stephan James and more also starring.

Paramount Pictures’ “Ebenezer” took the No. 3 spot with $2.04 million from 3,545 North American theaters in its second weekend in theaters. The Johnny Depp-led drama is eyeing another $7.775 million by Sunday, bringing its cumulative gross to $32.62 million.

“Ebenezer” reimagines the Christmas classic “A Christmas Carol,” this time starring Depp as Scrooge. Directed by Ti West, the description simply reads: “The name you know, the story you don’t.” Alongside Depp, “Ebenezer” boasts an ensemble including Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley, Arthur Conti, Ellie Bamber, Henry Lloyd-Hughes, Charlie Murphy, Tramell Tillman and Ian McKellen.

“The Cat in the Hat” followed in fourth place with $1.6 million from 3,26 locations. Rival estimates expect Warner Bros.’ animated film to add $7 million by Sunday, bringing the animated film’s cumulative gross to $47.26 million.

Bill Hader voices the titular character in the cartoon, which follows the shenanigans that occur after a mischievous, hat-wearing cat arrives to cheer up two siblings who move to a new town.

Finally, in fifth place was Columbia Pictures’ “Ghost Soldier.” The William Eubank-directed film earned $700,000 on Friday, coming in just ahead of GKids’ “Godzilla Minus Zero,” which brought in $680,000 on Friday. That puts the “Godzilla Minus One” follow-up at more than $51 million domestically.

Common Space has chosen Satellogic to build and operate its first high-resolution Earth-observing spacecraft.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first satellite in a constellation designed for humanitarian use will lift off next year, if all goes according to plan.

The nonprofit Common Space plans to assemble a six-spacecraft constellation of Earth-observing satellites, whose high-resolution imagery will aid first responders, journalists, scientists and human-rights investigators around the world.

That plan firmed up a bit today (Nov. 19), as Common Space announced the builder of the first of those satellites: Satellogic, an Argentine-U.S. geospatial intelligence company.

There are more than 1,000 Earth-observing satellites circling our planet at the moment. But much of the data they gather is proprietary or too expensive to serve the common good, according to Common Space.

The nonprofit wants to change that via its envisioned constellation, which it says will collect imagery specifically for humanitarian and public-interest purposes. Common Space plans to operate on a "club-good model," which will share infrastructure and costs across a large community, allowing extensive, low-cost access to high-quality imagery.

Satellogic is now officially part of this picture.

"With Satellogic as our spacecraft partner, we're moving from vision to orbit and putting high-resolution data into the hands of those who need it most," Common Space co-founder Rhiannan Price said in a statement today. "This isn't just another satellite. We're building infrastructure to serve people for years to come."

The satellite is Satellogic's NewSat Mark V, which Common Space selected after a competitive request-for-proposal process.

The NewSat Mark V is just 32 inches (82 centimeters) long and weighs 85 pounds (38.5 kilograms) here on Earth. But the microsatellite packs a great deal of capability into that small package. From low Earth orbit (LEO), it naturally resolves features on the ground as small as 27.5 inches (70 cm), which Satellogic's proprietary algorithms can boost to a "super resolution" of 19.7 inches (50 cm).

The satellite is scheduled to launch in July 2027, on a rocket that has yet to be announced. Satellogic will handle the preparations for that launch and manage satellite operations, which are expected to last at least five years in LEO. The company has extensive experience with such work; it has flown 61 of its Earth-observing satellites to date, all of which deployed successfully.

And Satellogic is aligned with Common Space philosophically, the company stressed.

"Common Space shares our belief that persistent global intelligence shouldn't be reserved for a few. Humanitarian responders and journalists are often first on the ground and last to get access, yet they need frequent, high-resolution imagery to see what's really happening so they can act with confidence," Luciano Giesso, vice president of space systems at Satellogic, said in the same statement. "This mission puts our vision of democratized access into practice."

Common Space is currently raising money to expand the constellation to six satellites, which it hopes to have in place by 2030. This will allow daily high-resolution coverage of "priority areas," according to the nonprofit.

Editor's note: The original version of this story stated that the first Satellogic satellite will launch on a SpaceX rocket. This information was in an embargoed version of today's press release but was not in the final version, so it has been removed from this story.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#672. How This Year’s Movies From ‘Artificial’ to ‘I Play Rocky’ Turn Political Anxiety Into Compelling Stories

For years, Simon Rich wanted to sound the alarm about AI.Rich’s childhood friend Dan Selsam worked as a researcher at OpenAI; Selsam showed Rich, a writer known for humorous essays and for the film “An American Pickle,” an early version of the software, and the two friends discussed its ramifications.“It seemed to have real contempt for mankind,” Rich says. “It scared the hell out of me.” Rich published a book, “which was completely ignored,” and found himself striking out in his attempts to get attention with magazine articles. “So, in desperation,” he recalls, “I was like, ‘Maybe if I got a movie star…’”He got Andrew Garfield. In “Artificial,” Garfield plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as a blithely destructive sociopath who manipulates his way into the center of a potentially civilization-ending technological advance. Rich uses the juicy character to tell a story about the most consequential political issue of the present moment.“I’ve been living with knowledge of this danger for at least five years, due to my fluke friendship with this scientist,” he says. (Selsam issued a public warning about AI’s increasingly uncontrollable behavior in September.) “I wrote this film out of a desperation to communicate to the world this information.”That desperation may be unique to Rich. But the desire to use the tools of screenwriting to illuminate political concerns is certainly not. Had “Artificial” simply been an enumeration of AI’s dangers, it’d likely have attracted as much attention as Rich’s book; instead, it’s a well-told story with a sharp argument at its core. That makes it one of several movies this year that use character and incident — the stuff of quality storytelling — to illuminate their writers’ very real political concerns.That goes for the year’s most-discussed blockbusters: Writer-director Christopher Nolan has imbued “The Odyssey” with a rueful sense of what it means to lose one’s humanity in wartime, while, if it’s anything like its two predecessor films, “Dune: Part Three,” written by Denis Villeneuve and Brian K. Vaughan, promises to examine the uses, and misuses, of power.But it’s showing up across more human-scale dramas this fall, as well. Take “I Play Rocky.” The film depicts the writing and production of “Rocky,” which — before it was an Oscar-winning smash — was the Hail Mary attempt of unknown actor Sylvester Stallone (played by Anthony Ippolito) to write himself a place in the industry. For screenwriter Peter Gamble, the story has resonances well beyond Hollywood history.“‘Rocky’ came out right after the Vietnam War, and it was a time when people needed to believe,” Gamble says. Stallone, in the film’s telling, is the ultimate underdog; Gamble, who himself yearned for a screenwriting breakout, could relate. The message of the film, the writer says, is intended in part for his children: “They’re like, ‘We’re all going to die from global warming. If not, AI is going to kill us next week.’ What power do I have in the universe at all? We need to believe in ourselves again.”American history provides many stories that feel akin to the charged atmosphere of recent years: One, as Gamble notes, is the demoralization of the Vietnam War, and another is the cataclysm of the Great Depression. “The Weight,” written by Matthew Booi and Shelby Gaines, is a rip-roaring adventure film in which unjustly imprisoned convict Samuel Murphy (Ethan Hawke) has the chance to win his freedom by transporting gold bricks across an unruly wilderness. The viewer roots for Murphy in part because he’s compellingly played by a movie star, and in part because the boot under which he struggles looks, at a moment of increased attention to mass incarceration and wealth inequality, familiar.“You don’t want it to be didactic and message-y or preachy in any way,” Gaines says. “But the idea was to try and tell a good story on a personal, individual level and hope that it would echo sympathetically with things that happen on a larger social level — both during the Great Depression and today.” Murphy’s journey depicts the stakes of its historical moment in frankly personal terms — his loss of freedom means the loss of access to his daughter, a crisis the film treats with gravity and righteous anger.“Abstraction doesn’t help you as a writer much,” Gaines says. “If you want to convey something, the heart is the place to start.”Or you can go for the gut. “Ink,” which James Graham adapted from his own stage play, makes the case that Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) and newspaper editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) created the venal media world we live in today. The dawning realization that Lamb, especially, is a force for evil hits particularly hard because Graham has, in the film’s early going, taken pains to make him so charming and his exploits so rootable.“You need these people to surprise you,” Graham says, “so that you want to be in that newsroom — and suddenly, weirdly, for a brief moment, you might even want them to get one over on the establishment.” How did tabloid culture gain such purchase? Because, as the film’s characters make clear, we’re willing to pay for it.“Being Heumann” makes us root for its band of rebels, too — but, in this case, they’re working to bring about a better world. The biopic, written by Sian Heder and Rebekah Taussig, tells the story of Judith Heumann (Ruth Madeley), the activist who led the 1977 demonstration over the government’s failure to enforce disability-rights legislation. By its nature, the film is explicitly political, but its screenplay is also the product of a thoughtful, careful approach to representation and inclusivity.Taussig, who, like the late Heumann, uses a wheelchair, saw a certain power in learning about — and then writing about — the many activists Heumann helped organize. “What was so exciting about the research,” she says, “was this gold mine of learning about these absolutely compelling people.”The first-time screenwriter had grown up seeing “very little disability representation — and [when there was], it always felt so flat. There is a richness to the experience of disability that gets missed if you don’t live it and you can’t portray it.”Taussig’s ability to mine her own insights enriches the film, one that Heder, an Oscar-winner for “CODA,” intended to inspire and delight audiences, as well as educate them. “It’s very important to me that this story reach the widest audience possible,” Heder says, “because the events of the story actually were about a triumph. In a time where a lot of us are feeling really helpless, it was so important to express disabled joy and humor. I wanted to take the audience on a really entertaining ride, where they could leave seeing the world differently.”“Fjord” has a similar reframing effect — though its true-life basis is substantially more downbeat than Judith Heumann’s story. Cristian Mungiu took inspiration from the story of the Bodnariu family, an immigrant couple whose five children were taken away by the Norwegian state amid accusations of child abuse. “Fjord” presents the story of Mihai and Lisbet Gheorghiu (Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve) in a who-do-you-believe social drama, one with painful repercussions.“What I’m looking into, in the stories that I pick up,” Mungiu says, “is this possibility of speaking about something bigger than just that story.” For its writer-director, “Fjord” addresses the painful consequences of globalization, as people from different traditions find that they cannot in fact understand one another. “It’s not a reenactment” of the Bodnariu story, he says: “That’s the starting point of a story in which everything is structured to speak about the relationship between the majority and the individual.”“Fjord” won the top prize at this year’s Cannes; the runner-up, “Minotaur,” also places a family drama in counterpoint with a story of major import. Here, a story of marital infidelity (based on Claude Chabrol’s 1969 film “The Unfaithful Wife”) plays out in 2022 as Russia is scaling up its military actions against Ukraine.Writer-director Andrey Zvyagintsev had been working to put the film together for years — and, as he wrote, the mobilization against Ukraine was all over the news. “It was a very logical thing,” he says through a translator. “I started to fill gaps in the script with the realities of what was happening.” Like Simon Rich trying to spread the word against AI, Zvyagintsev used his script to convey what he was hearing, like local mayors asking businesspeople to choose which of their employees will be conscripted. “This is not something I took from the air,” Zvyagintsev says. “This is real information that came by phone. People would be afraid to speak up about those situations.”For Zvyagintsev, this use of character to explore the world around him is what screenwriting is all about. “The whole ocean,” he says, “can be reflected in one ocean drop.” Related Stories YouTube Refuses U.K. Government Request to Remove Russell Brand Video, Says It Is Investigating Content Emma Chamberlain, Wesley Wang, Aryna Sabalenka and More Unveil New Projects for YouTube

#671. A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising new way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Researchers have discovered that increasing levels of this protein can reduce the buildup of toxic tangles associated with brain damage, while also helping preserve the connections that allow nerve cells to communicate.

The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to new treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. In experiments with mice, the researchers found that boosting the protein reduced several damaging changes associated with Alzheimer's, including brain shrinkage and the accumulation of abnormal tau proteins.

The discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning. Under normal conditions, tau proteins help stabilize microtubules, tiny structures that provide internal support to neurons and help maintain the intricate networks of the nervous system.

In Alzheimer's and several related disorders, however, tau proteins can become abnormal and stick together, forming harmful clumps known as tau tangles. These tangles disrupt the normal functioning of nerve cells and are associated with cognitive decline and neuronal death. Diseases characterized by abnormal tau accumulation are collectively called tauopathies.

A Protective Protein With a Surprising Role in Alzheimer's

The researchers investigated a protein called sorting-related receptor with A-type repeats (SORLA), which has already attracted scientific attention for its potential role in protecting the brain against Alzheimer's disease.

Previous studies have shown that SORLA can help limit the production and accumulation of amyloid-beta, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's. Amyloid-beta can build up into plaques in the brain, making it one of the disease's major pathological hallmarks alongside tau tangles.

"In the last 15 or 20 years, considerable data has come out from our lab and other groups showing that SORLA can suppress one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease -- amyloid-beta generation and accumulation," said Timothy Huang, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.

"Very little was known, however, about whether SORLA affected the tau tangles reflected on the other side of the coin in Alzheimer's disease."

To investigate this question, the scientists developed a mouse model by breeding animals engineered to produce additional human SORLA with mice that develop tau tangles, brain atrophy, and cognitive impairments. This allowed them to examine whether higher SORLA levels could reduce tau accumulation and protect against the damage it causes.

Boosting SORLA Reduces Toxic Tau and Brain Shrinkage

The results revealed that additional SORLA provided protection against several processes that contribute to tau tangles and the progression of neurodegenerative disease.

One important effect involved a process called hyperphosphorylation. This occurs when too many phosphate groups attach to tau proteins, altering their behavior and contributing to the development of harmful tangles. Higher SORLA levels reduced this abnormal modification.

The protein also limited the ability of misfolded tau to act as "seeds" that encourage other tau proteins to clump together. This seeding process can help toxic tau aggregates multiply and spread their damaging effects.

Beyond reducing tau abnormalities, SORLA helped preserve synapses, the specialized connections through which neurons communicate. It also protected synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or modify those connections, which is essential for learning, memory, and normal cognitive function.

"When you upregulate SORLA, you can suppress the negative effects found in tauopathies," said Huijie Huang, PhD, a staff scientist in the Huang lab at Sanford Burnham Prebys and lead author of the study.

"We found there was less brain atrophy and less tau accumulation, which was very exciting to see."

Removing the Protein Makes Brain Damage Worse

After observing the benefits of increasing SORLA, the researchers examined what would happen if the protein were missing entirely.

SORLA is produced using instructions encoded by a gene called Sorl1. Some people carry mutations that interfere with this gene's function, potentially disrupting the production or activity of the protective protein.

To investigate the consequences, the team studied genetically modified mice that lacked Sorl1 and therefore could not produce SORLA.

The results contrasted sharply with those seen in mice carrying additional copies of the protein. Instead of protecting against tau-related damage, the absence of SORLA made the harmful effects more severe.

"The opposite turned out to be true when we deleted the ability to produce SORLA proteins," said Tim Huang, senior and corresponding author of the manuscript. "A lack of SORLA exacerbated the harmful effects observed in tauopathies."

These contrasting results provided further evidence that SORLA plays an important protective role in the brain and may influence how severely tau-related diseases progress.

A New Clue Could Lead to Alzheimer's Treatments

To understand why changing SORLA levels had such different effects, the researchers examined the molecular activity of individual brain cells and the surrounding tissue.

They combined advanced sequencing methods to measure protein levels and gene activity in individual cells with techniques that map where RNA and proteins are located within brain tissue. This detailed approach helped reveal how SORLA influences the biological processes involved in neurodegeneration.

The analysis showed that increasing SORLA helped prevent harmful changes in protein production at synapses while also suppressing other mechanisms associated with tauopathy progression.

The researchers also discovered that higher SORLA levels reduced abnormal gene activity in glial cells. These cells perform several essential functions in the nervous system, including supporting, maintaining, and protecting neurons. Changes in glial cell activity can contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.

One finding was especially intriguing because it pointed toward a potential target for existing medications.

"One particularly notable finding that we can build on is the upregulation of a member of the plexin-B family of receptors in the absence of SORLA," said Huijie Huang.

Plexin-B receptors are proteins involved in cellular signaling, helping cells respond to information from their surroundings. The increased activity of a receptor in this family when SORLA was absent suggests that this signaling pathway could be involved in some of the damaging changes associated with tau disorders.

Importantly, drugs capable of targeting this family of receptors already exist, raising the possibility that scientists could investigate whether they might be useful against tau-related dementia.

"There are unique drugs that can target this class of receptors that we may be able to apply to tau-related dementia disorders," said Tim Huang. "One potential future direction is to repurpose these drugs to target overactivation of glial cells and perhaps reverse some of the phenotypes in tauopathies."

The Next Step Toward Human Alzheimer's Research

Although the findings are encouraging, the protective effects were demonstrated in mice, and more research is needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans.

The team now hopes to investigate how individual types of brain cells respond when SORLA levels increase or decrease. One planned approach involves transplanting human neurons or glial cells into mouse brains, allowing researchers to examine the effects of different SORLA mutations in a living brain affected by disease.

"Mouse cells and human cells are different," said Tim Huang. "Because we're looking at human disease, it's more informative if we can observe the modulation and dysfunction of SORLA in the context of a human cell inside of a diseased brain environment."

These experiments could help clarify how SORLA protects neurons from toxic tau accumulation and why disruptions in its function make neurodegeneration worse.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that a deeper understanding of this protective protein will reveal new treatment strategies, either by enhancing SORLA's activity or by repurposing existing drugs to interfere with damaging cellular pathways. Such approaches could eventually offer new ways to combat Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia driven by toxic tau tangles.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute and National Institute on Aging.

#670. Germany news: Merz, Söder aim to revisit electricity tax cut

The Christian Democrats are in Munich, pushing to revive some tax relief that didn't make it into the budget after talks last week. And Manuela Schwesig faces a vote on a new term as regional leader. Follow DW.

Stay tuned for more on these stories and anything else in or concerning Germany on November 16, 2026.

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow. Bis dann!

Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.

It was the team's sixth game under head coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.

Germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.

Speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game, attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half."

Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.

Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.

By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.

Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who has come under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025, and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany.

"We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," said Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team."

A group of five EU member states, including Germany, have entered talks over a scheme to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.

The plan to set up so-called return hubs in a non-EU country had been announced by the group — which also includes Austria, the Netherlands, Greece and Denmark — had first been announced back in September.

Tesla has earmarked some €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory in Germany, near to Berlin.

The Grünheide complex will be expanded to start producing the electric car company's driverless Cybercabs, with output expected to eventually reach 1 million units.

The Elon Musk-owned company said construction would begin in 2027, with the first Cybercabs rolling off the line in 2029.

"With this, we are laying the foundations for the world's most technologically advanced Tesla factory here in Grünheide," Tesla said.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Matt Pearson on our sports desk breaks down where the power struggle currently stands, with the deadline for candiates just a matter of hours away now.

Lawmakers in the state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have voted in Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier.

The 52-year-old has been in the role since 2017 and is heading into a third term.

The vote was a secret ballot, but it can still be assumed who voted and how.

She received 39 of the 68 votes cast in the chamber, exactly as many as commanded by Schwesig's three-party coaliton of her Social Democrats (29), the ecologist Greens (5), and the socialist Left Party (5).

While Söder's comments in Munich focused in particular on the policy the coalition in Berlin had not delivered, Merz initiatlly focused on talking up the efficacy of his federal coalition.

"We are aware of the situation. We know that we now need to deliver. And we also know that we face difficult talks within the coalition. But I would also say from the experiences of the last weeks that there are solutions to the problems which we have in Germany," Merz said.

Merz said that in the 18 months since last year's election, the coalition "has already successfully implemented many things, not 'set them into motion' as people like to say, but actually implemented."

He noted a total of 17 bills going through the second and third reading process in the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, last week, "including the most comprehensive reforms of our intelligence and security services that we have ever done in [post-war] Germany."

Among others, he thanked Bavarian Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a senior member of the Bavarian CSU sister party to Merz's own conservative CDU, for his contribution to this.

Merz also touted the support given to CSU politician Ilse Aigner, not just from his CDU but from the Social Democrat coalition partners and the Greens, to become the next president, calling her a person who would "represent our country very well at home and abroad."

After hailing these accomplishments, Merz then turned to electricity tax cuts, saying he anticipated talks on the matter on Tuesday that would be "very short."

He said that over the weekend, coalition leaders had revisited the figures, and now believed they would be able to "completely" reduce electricity taxes to the minimum European levels in 2027 "also for private households."

Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has appeared with Friedrich Merz at a press conference during the chancellor's trip to Munich.

It seems Söder, Merz and the CDU/CSU believe they have unfinished business after the budget was finalized in the Bundestag late last week.

Merz had pledged in the run-up to the decision to provide a reduction in electricity tax for all, but the final agreement did not include this step, with the coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) saying it was not adequately costed.

Söder said he and Merz had discussed "backup for the coming days," for Berlin and for a "collective stance, that is really, really important."

He said the coming days were about "demonstrating credibility in politics," seemingly in reference to Merz's promise that the coalition did not ultimately deliver.

"That's why it's really important to us that we do indeed bring about the reduction in electricity tax," Söder said. "This is important for businesses. It would be a relief for citizens. But it's also a matter of credibility and it's written in the coalition agreement."

Söder said that as to the question of "where the money comes from, with a €560 billion (roughly $615 billion) budget, with €200 billion in new debt, nobody can tell me there's no potential within the budgeting process."

A festive piece of merchandise on the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) "fan shop" website has upset some religious leaders in Germany.

Called a "chocolate Nicholas," it appears to depict a semblance of Saint Nicholas in bishop's regalia and the party's colors and holding a book with "AfD" written on the cover where a Bible might be in more traditional iconography.

The Bishop of Essen, Franz-Josef Overbeck, was highly critical of the promotion in Monday's edition of the Bild newspaper.

"The AfD is appropriating Christian symbols for party campaigning," Overbeck said. "Showing the holy Nicholas in a blue coat with mitre, staff and the gospel with an AfD logo is not in order."

Overbeck acknowledged that other organizations like football clubs would sell chocolate Christmas figurines in club colors, but he said they would tend to refrain from including overtly Christian symbols when doing so.

Bild quoted an AfD spokesman as saying that as a "liberal-conservative party that clearly associates itself with Christian values," the item fit "particularly well" with the party image.

The main German protestant church group EKD's cultural representative, Johann Hinrich Claussen, said the offer showed the AfD had "no understanding of traditions and no respect" for Christianity.

He described the action as "embarrassing and revealing," and said that Christianity was "supra-partisan."

"The AfD knows little about what is holy to Christians. Otherwise, it would be aware that Bishop Nicholas of Myra, in what today is Demre in Turkey, stood clearly for uniting the occident and the orient. Beyond that, he is the patron saint of rescues at sea," Claussen said.

The partner of deceased Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger has said that anybody is welcome at his funeral this coming Saturday.

Aiwanger was the economy minister in Bavaria's state government as the leader of the junior coalition partners to the center-right CSU.

"Hubert was a man of the people and so it stands to reason that anyone who liked or treaasured him is allowed to come to his funeral," Tanja Schweiger wrote on her Instagram profile overnight.

She was posting after a requiem in the state capital Munich paying tribute to the leader of the Free Voters (Freie Wähler) party over the weekend. Around 1,100 people attended this ceremony.

Aiwanger died suddenly and unexpectedly on November 4 during a working visit to Berlin, aged 55.

Prosecutors have since said he died of natural causes, after he was found dead in his hotel room.

Germany's national men's football team will play neighbors and rivals the Netherlands for the 50th time on Monday night.

And there's quite a lot at stake for Jürgen Klopp's team in the last group stage game of the Nations League competition at Berlin's Olympiastadion.

If Germany win, they will qualify for the knockout stages, but a defeat could lead to potential relegation into the second tier of Nations League football.

Klopp was upbeat in the pre-match press conference at the prospect of playing the Netherlands, who he said play "Xavi football," in the image of the skillful Spanish playmaker and World Cup winner coaching the team.

"I've always loved playing against teams like this. For all my coaching career," Klopp said. "When someone says, 'hey they can really play football,' then in my mind the party's already started."

A full house with some 71,000 fans is expected in the capital when the game kicks off. Klopp played on the Dutch reputation for liberal use of bicylces in his comments to reporters, saying he wanted to "put a stick in their spokes" and dislodge them from the saddle.

The notion of a bridge over the valley between Ratingen and Heiligenhaus to the east of Düsseldorf in western Germany as part of the A44 highway is more than half a century old. And the physical bridge itself has stood, complete, ever since 2022.

Yet still the crossing is not connected to any roads at either end.

A construction project to build the last 4.4 kilometers of highway and link the bridge to the A44 highway will formally start on Monday.

State premier Hendrik Wüst, as well as the regional transport and traffic ministers will attend the ground-breaking ceremony.

A project first conceived some 55 years ago has faced repeated delays because of lawsuits, environmental protection studies and onerous planning and permit procedures.

The bridge across the Angerbachtal (Angerbach Valley) should improve the road connection between the North Rhine-Westphalia state capital of Düsseldorf, the Bergisches Land mountain range and the industrial cities in the Ruhr Valley. It's also meant to help remove some strain from the perenially busy A3 highway and to improve the road connections to Düsseldorf International Airport.

The last stretch of highway is expected to cost around €200 million (roughly $220 million), or roughly the annual costs incurred each year by forcing traffic to divert around it, according to estimates from Düsseldorf's IHK industry and trade association.

Construction is expected to take several years, no formal end date has yet been set.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz heads to Munich early on Monday, for a meeting with the leadership of the Bavarian Christian Social Democrats (CSU), the sister party to his conservative  Christian Democrats(CDU).

No concrete details about the talks were made public ahead of time, except for the CSU saying it would serve as a general exchange that had been planned for some time.

The trip comes a week after Merz nominated Ilse Aigner as the next German president, likely paving the way for her to become the first woman and first CSU politician to assume the role.

It also follows soon after the 2027 federal budget cleared a marathon meeting of the parliamentary budget committee in Berlin. This serves as one of the more conspicuous examples of the frictions and difficulties in the grand coalition between the Christian Democrats and the center-left Social Democrats — with the compromises it contains a point of frustration among the CSU and for state premier Markus Söder.

The northeastern state parliament in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will likely vote in Social Democrat (SPD) Manuela Schwesig for another term as state premier early in the afternoon.

The 52-year-old, who first stepped into the role in 2017, plans to lead a new coalition of the SPD, the environmentalist Greens and the socialist Left Party after state elections in September.

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) emerged as the largest single party in the sparsely populated state.

But still, the political calculus that emerged was arguably simpler than in Berlin — where the socialist Left Party is the largest party but could struggle to lead a coaltion — and in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD was by far the largest party but short of an outright majority.

Schwesig's SPD claimed 29 seats, with the Greens and the Left each taking 5, meaning that when combined, they hold a fairly clear majority over the AfD with its 32 seats.

The SPD's relatively successful performance in the state, at least compared to its national struggles, has also led to Schwesig being linked with a possible return to federal politics. The SPD plans to elect a new leadership duo early next year.

Schwesig has already had a spell in Berlin as the federal minsiter for families, pensioners and women, and briefly led the SPD on an interim basis in 2017, but after this she returned to her home state to seek the top regional job instead.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Servus! Welcome to another Monday of news and analysis of matters making waves in German politics and society.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is starting his week in Munich, at a meeting of the Bavarian CSU sister party to his conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).

This comes a few days after Merz naming CSU politician Ilse Aigner as candidate to be the next president, and days after the budget committee signed off on the federal government's spending plans for 2027. Merz is expected to appear with state premier Markus Söder in a joint press conference later.

Far to the north, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Social Democrat Manuela Schwesig should be voted in for another term as state premier in the regional parliament later in the day. Schwesig emerged in pole position after state elections a few weeks ago; some suspect her regional success could translate into national ambitions within the struggling party.

And in the west, regional leaders are headed to a road to nowhere — literally, but also hopefully not for very much longer now.

The vast highway A44 bridge over the valley between Helsinghausen and Ratingen-Ost has been planned for decades, and was completed in 2022, but work to actually connect it to the road network will only start today.

Stay with us for more on these stories and whatever else develops around Germany on November 16.

From colorful meteors to lingering trails, the Leonids put on a great show this year.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Leonid meteor shower put on quite the show this week, with bright, colorful meteors thrilling stargazers worldwide and we've got the photos to prove it.

The annual meteor shower peaked overnight on Nov. 17-18, with photographers braving chilly temperatures, clouds and even fog in hopes of catching the perfect shot. And for some, their patience certainly paid off.

Leonids occur when Earth passes through debris left behind by comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. As tiny pieces of comet debris enter Earth's atmosphere at speeds of up to 44 miles (71 kilometers) per second, they burn up, producing bright streaks of light.

The meteor shower is also famous for producing some of the most spectacular meteor storms in history. In fact, this year marks the 60th anniversary of the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966, when observers reported an astonishing 40 meteors per second at the peak. To mark the occasion, we spoke to people who witnessed the extraordinary event first-hand and you can read their remarkable accounts in our special feature.

But back to the present! Let's take a look at some of the best photographs and videos captured during this year's impressive display.

Photographer Austin Rebello drove several hours to Nubble Lighthouse in York, Maine, to meet up with fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright and hopefully capture a Leonid or two.

"I specifically drove a few hours up there for hopes of capturing exactly this, as the radiant of the Leonids rose behind the lighthouse," Rebello told Space.com in an email.

"My friend and I were lucky enough to also see it with our eyes, and it was definitely a top 3 meteor for me, as it was even bright enough to briefly cast shadows."

Rebello also revealed on X that the meteor left behind a vibrant blue trail that remained visible to the naked eye for more than 30 seconds.

Fellow astrophotographer Rob Wright was also at Nubble Lighthouse that night, where he captured the lingering trail of a particularly bright meteor on camera for an incredible 12 minutes, according to a post on X.

"Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there," Wright wrote on X.

Turns out the smoke from the bright meteor early this morning was visible on camera for TWELVE (12) MINUTES just lingering there. I was able to make a rough timelapse video to show this. -- November 18, 2026 York, Maine https://t.co/pm9htHcMm3November 18, 2026

This phenomenon is known as a persistent meteor train and is created when a bright meteor leaves behind a trail of ionized gas that continues to glow long after the meteor itself has disappeared. These ghostly trails usually fade relatively quickly, but some, like this one, can persist for several minutes. They can twist and change shape as they're carried along by winds high in Earth's atmosphere, according to the BBC Sky at Night Magazine.

Meanwhile, over Deming, New Mexico, photographer Greg Gage had to contend with rather less favorable conditions as clouds and unexpected fog rolled in during the meteor shower's peak.

"While it was perfectly clear when I set up the camera, the night turned out to be mostly cloudy with some light fog," Gage told Space.com in an email.

"But it was just a thin veil and made for some interesting effects. I did catch one meteor through the fog."

But the fog wasn't the only surprise Gage encountered. He also managed to capture a particularly colorful meteor as it blazed through the sky.

"One meteor was rather dramatic. It went through multiple colors as it traveled through the atmosphere," Gage continued.

Gage captured the photographs with a Nikon D5500 and a 14mm lens.

And the colorful displays weren't limited to North America.

In Japan, astronomer Daichi Fujii, curator of the Hiratsuka City Museum, captured a spectacular Leonid fireball streaking across the sky above Hiratsuka in the early hours of Nov. 19.

The brilliant fireball left behind a glowing trail that changed from green to orange as it lingered in the sky.

A fireball is defined as an unusually bright meteor that reaches a visual magnitude of -3 or brighter, according to NASA's Center for Near Earth Object Studies.

Elsewhere in Japan, skywatcher @simao had a particularly productive night, capturing an impressive 92 meteors between 10:17 p.m. local time on Nov. 18 and 5:40 a.m. on Nov. 19, from central Saitama Prefecture.

昨夜から今朝にかけて捉えた流星は正味92個でした。 11/18 22:17 〜 11/19 05:40 埼玉県中央から #atomcam #meteordetect #火球 #流星 https://t.co/jRzsHdQ7MVNovember 19, 2026

But that wasn't all simao captured that night! At 2:19 a.m. on Nov. 19, they caught both a Leonid meteor and a sprite at the same time, looking northwest.

Sprites are very difficult to capture, as they appear as fleeting flashes of light high above thunderstorms, typically appearing as red, jellyfish-like structures.

昨夜の流星とスプライト、初めて同じタイミングで撮れた。 11/19 02:19:36 埼玉県中央から北西の空 #atomcam #meteordetect #火球 #流星 #スプライト https://t.co/LBipTuoM0LNovember 19, 2026

The Leonids were already making an appearance in the days leading up to the shower's peak.

On Nov. 16, astrophotographer @EricTheSpaceCat captured several possible Leonids streaking through the sky.

Meteors from last night/this morning. Cropped to show detail. A lot of possible Leonids. The Leonid meteor shower is active and peaks the night of 11/17-11/18. https://t.co/s7YsvKdvECNovember 15, 2026

A likely Leonid meteor from yesterday morning. The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight! Good luck if you go out to watch. https://t.co/xxbEV32NQlNovember 17, 2026

If the Leonids have left you wanting more, you won't have to wait long for another significant meteor shower! Next up are the Geminids, one of the most prolific meteor showers of the year, which will peak overnight on Dec. 13-14. And 2026 is shaping up to be a particularly good year for them. With only a slender waxing crescent moon in the sky, moonlight interference will be minimal, giving skywatchers a chance to spot up to 120 Geminid meteors per hour under ideal conditions.

For the best views, head somewhere dark, away from city lights, and give your eyes around 30 minutes to adjust to the darkness.

#668. Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds

Vitamin C may do more than support everyday health. New research from the University of Waterloo suggests that it could also help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming during digestion. Using mathematical modeling, scientists investigated how vitamin C influences chemical reactions in the digestive system that have been linked to cancer risk.

Exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades. These compounds are found in cured meats such as bacon and salami, as well as in fruits and vegetables grown in soil or water affected by pollution. Although nitrates and nitrites contribute to important functions in the brain and cardiovascular system, they can also participate in potentially harmful reactions once they reach the stomach.

One of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development. Understanding what causes these chemicals to form, and what might prevent their formation, has been a longstanding challenge.

Why Vitamin C Could Change the Cancer Risk Equation

"Since at least the 90s, researchers have been studying the link between cancer and these compounds, with conflicting results," said Dr. Gordon McNicol, a post-doctoral researcher in applied mathematics and the first author of the study. "Our work suggests that the presence of dietary Vitamin C may help explain these inconsistencies."

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body and undergo chemical changes. The model incorporated several interconnected systems, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

Their simulations revealed that vitamin C consumed alongside nitrates and nitrites may interfere with the formation of potentially harmful compounds. This could help explain why foods containing nitrates do not necessarily carry the same risks.

For example, leafy vegetables such as spinach naturally contain both nitrates and vitamin C. According to the model, the presence of vitamin C could limit the chemical reactions associated with cancer risk, potentially helping explain the protective effects suggested by some dietary research.

The researchers also explored whether vitamin C supplements might offer similar benefits when taken after eating.

Their findings suggest that taking vitamin C after each meal could moderately reduce the formation of nitrosation products associated with cancer risk. This effect could be particularly relevant when consuming foods containing nitrates and nitrites, including processed meats such as bacon and salami.

However, the results come from mathematical simulations rather than clinical trials. Although the model predicts that vitamin C can reduce the production of potentially harmful chemicals, further research is needed to determine whether this translates into a measurable reduction in cancer risk in humans.

New Clues for Future Cancer Prevention Research

The researchers believe their model could help scientists better understand the complicated relationship between diet, digestive chemistry, and cancer risk. It may also provide guidance for future experiments examining how nutritional choices influence the formation of potentially harmful compounds.

"This work provides a mechanistic roadmap for future clinical and laboratory studies by identifying the key interacting drivers of these potentially harmful chemical reactions, including nitrite exposure, antioxidant intake, meal timing, gastric conditions and oral microbiome activity," said Dr. Anita Layton, professor of applied mathematics and Canada 150 researcher chair. "This model can help researchers design more targeted experiments and interventions, focusing on when and in whom nitrosation is most likely to occur."

By identifying how factors such as vitamin C intake, meal timing, stomach conditions, and bacteria in the mouth interact, the model could help researchers develop more precise strategies for studying and potentially reducing cancer-related chemical reactions during digestion.

The study, "Vitamin C as a nitrosation inhibitor: A modelling study across dietary patterns and water quality," was published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.

Materials provided by University of Waterloo. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#667. CAA’s Bryan Lourd Urges Congress to Pass NO FAKES Act to Combat AI Deepfakes: ‘Every One of Us Should Have the Right to Say No’

Creative Arts Agency CEO Bryan Lourd urged Congress on Saturday to pass the NO FAKES Act, a bill that would regulate the wave of unauthorized AI deepfakes proliferating the internet, writing in a New York Times Opinion piece that “every one of us should have the right to say no to an unwelcome use of our likeness.”

The NO FAKES Act was introduced by Sen. Chris Coons (D-ME) in May, following a previous attempt at the bill last year. While it advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee in June and has a bipartisan coalition of co-sponsors, the full Senate has not taken it up. Lourd wrote that the bill would introduce a federal standard for “control, consent and compensation” surrounding deepfakes, replacing “outdated, ill-fitting state laws, many of them written with an analog world in mind.” Related Stories Creators Pounce on Midterm Elections, Hoping to Win New Viewers and More Dollars YouTube Refuses U.K. Government Request to Remove Russell Brand Video, Says It Is Investigating Content

“I come to this issue not as a policymaker but as a practitioner. I run a global talent agency. Part of our job is to help our clients license their likenesses and performances, sometimes to AI companies,” he added. “We regularly negotiate those deals, and I can tell you that the bill pending in Congress delivers what the industry needs and what will protect all Americans.”

Lourd laid out the stakes for Hollywood by citing Tom Hanks, who warned his followers in 2023 about a dental office using an AI deepfake of a younger version of him in an advertisement. Hanks likely wouldn’t have agreed to the dental ad, Lourd wrote, but he should’ve been given a choice before the dental office ran with an unauthorized deepfake.

“What’s missing is a bright-line rule affirming that right in the AI age, and it is one Congress can supply before the year is out,” Lourd wrote.

CAA has advocated against the unauthorized proliferation of celebrity deepfakes online, working with the Cate Blanchett-backed Human Consent Foundation to help people control permissions for their likenesses if they’re scraped by AI models. The agency also joined the foundation and other entertainment backers in an amicus brief in the New York Times’ lawsuit against OpenAI, noting the active licensing market for likenesses that’s developed in the AI era.

Deepfakes have been a constant presence since large-language models emerged in 2022, with many being used to produce unauthorized and sometimes explicit depictions of actors, singers and other celebrities. Other industry backers of the NO FAKES Act include SAG-AFTRA, the Motion Picture Association, the Recording Industry Association of America, the Recording Academy and the National Association of Broadcasters, OpenAI, the AFL-CIO, YouTube and IBM.

Buildings across the United States are celebrating Voyager 1's major milestone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Empire State Building glowed in glittering gold last night (Nov. 17) to celebrate NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hitting one light-day from Earth. And it isn't the only building celebrating this achievement with a sparkling display.

Today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit one light-day from Earth. About 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers) away, this is the point at which it takes a full day (or 24 hours) for one light particle to get from us to the probe. So any signal we send to Voyager 1 or it sends back now takes a full day as the spacecraft continues to explore interstellar space.

To celebrate the major milestone for the farthest human-made object in history, the Empire State Building in New York City lit up in gold. This golden glow references the Golden Record onboard both the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft.

And the Empire State Building wasn't the only major landmark to celebrate the occasion. The Space Needle in Seattle, Washington, and both the Willis Tower and the Skydeck Chicago in Chicago, Illinois have all been illuminated gold to mark the milestone.

The Golden Record that these gold glowing buildings are referencing serves as an inanimate ambassador for Earth, carrying information about humanity, our planet, the other species who live here, the languages we speak, the music we listen to and so much more. It even includes instructions for building a record player to play the record.

The Voyager mission has, and continues to, make incredible scientific discoveries and observations throughout our solar system and now in interstellar space. But this Golden Record provides an additional aspect to the mission that connects us here on Earth to whatever unknown life may exist out there.

If some sort of life forms out in the cosmos were to ever come across Voyager and its Golden Record at any point in the distant future, they might learn a little bit about our small blue dot.

With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. #664. A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain

Emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment. The findings, which will be presented at Neuroscience 2026, reveal important differences that could help researchers develop more personalized approaches to treating complex brain conditions. Neuroscience 2026 is the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and the world's largest source of emerging news about brain science and health.

Researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup. Understanding these differences could lead to treatments better suited to each individual's biology. Two conditions receiving particular attention are Alzheimer's disease (AD), an incurable disorder that progressively damages memory and other brain functions, and fibromyalgia, a chronic illness marked by persistent pain and fatigue that affects 2-4% of the global population. According to the World Health Organization, Alzheimer's affects between 35 and 40 million people worldwide.

Menopause, Genetics, and Alzheimer's Disease

Two of the new studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.

One investigation found that people carrying genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's responded differently to menopause hormone therapy (MHT) compared with those without the same genetic risks. The effects also varied according to the particular combination of hormones used. These findings suggest that both genetic background and hormone therapy formulation deserve consideration when evaluating treatment options. (Mateja Perović, University of Toronto)

A separate study examined rodents undergoing menopause that also carried genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's. Researchers observed that brain circuits responsible for memory became particularly vulnerable, providing evidence that menopause may represent an important period of increased susceptibility for women who are genetically predisposed to the disease. (Stephanie M. Perez, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio)

Sex Differences in Chronic Pain and Brain Inflammation

The other two studies explored how biological sex influences pain sensitivity, immune activity, and the effects of inflammation on the brain.

In a mouse model of fibromyalgia, females continued to show heightened sensitivity to touch and stronger immune system activation compared with males. The findings suggest that the biological processes contributing to chronic pain may differ between sexes, potentially making treatments tailored to these differences more effective. (Yasmin Sahlloul, University of Cincinnati)

Another investigation uncovered differences in how prolonged intestinal inflammation influences the brain. Using a mouse model, researchers found that chronic gut inflammation affected brain function and Alzheimer's related disease changes differently in males and females. The results provide additional evidence that biological sex may influence the relationship between inflammation and neurological disease. (Nurcan Kilic, University of North Dakota)

Toward More Personalized Treatments for Brain Disorders

Together, the four studies underscore the importance of examining sex and genetic differences when investigating neurological conditions. By identifying biological factors that influence disease progression and treatment responses, researchers hope to move toward more precise therapies for Alzheimer's, fibromyalgia, and other difficult-to-treat brain disorders.

"These four studies illustrate the fascinating discoveries that can be made when focusing on female-specific biology or possible sex differences in AD-related symptoms and risk factors," said Liisa Galea, PhD, Treliving Family Chair in Women's Mental Health at Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and moderator of the press conference. "The research presented at Neuroscience 2026 helps us pinpoint the specific differences that may help us develop more targeted treatment using precision approaches, even for some of our most complex brain disorders."

Materials provided by Society for Neuroscience. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#663. Celluloid Sounds: Fewer Women Composers on Screen, But Some Hit the Right Notes

The stats for women composers in Hollywood have not improved. Just eight of this year’s top 100 grossing films feature original scores by women; the past two years have seen percentages between 7 and 9%, all down from 14% in 2023.

But female composers continue to be in the awards conversation, and not all for their music. Laura Karpman, composer of “American Fiction” and the current Netflix miniseries “East of Eden,” has entered her first film as director in the documentary short subject category: “Cosmic Symphony.” Related Stories Creators Pounce on Midterm Elections, Hoping to Win New Viewers and More Dollars Emma Chamberlain, Wesley Wang, Aryna Sabalenka and More Unveil New Projects for YouTube

The film is a timely look at four musical artists who lost priceless, beloved instruments in the Palisades and Eaton fires of January 2025: composer Starr Parodi, whose 1928 Steinway piano was heard in dozens of MGM scores including “The Wizard of Oz”; songwriter Diane Warren, who lost a Yamaha grand; jazz bassist John Clayton, whose string bass was nearly 200 years old; and Altadena educator Susie Chung, whose brown Steinway was played by Lady Gaga in “A Star Is Born” and on the 2019 Oscarcast.

“I believe my piano has a soul… I have a little regret that I left her alone,” Chung says in the film, and that sentiment is echoed by the other musicians. “Instruments have hearts, they have souls, they have lives,” says Warren, a 17-time best song nominee. Two days before the fires, Warren was filmed performing her Oscar-nominated song “The Journey” on the piano in her Malibu beach house.

Clayton’s bass, once owned by the legendary Ray Brown, had accompanied Ella Fitzgerald, Frank Sinatra, Nat King Cole and Duke Ellington. Recalling its past, he said “that bass and the music that it made was bigger than any of us could ever be.”

Parodi describes her lost keyboard as having “this beautiful, haunting, bell-like sound… warm and thick,” and she tells the harrowing story of watching her house go up in flames via their doorbell camera and later unearthing the remains of her MGM piano in the rubble.

Thousands of instruments were reduced to ash during the L.A. fires. “I felt it was a story that was really important to be told,” Karpman says. “When you live with these instruments, they have personalities, they see history.”

In addition to the interviews and performance footage, she added lively, colorful animation to the story. Animator Tempe Hale sought “to make the instruments come alive again, (to convey) the kind of fun and glory and energy that these instruments have.”

Karpman also composed the score for her film, incorporating both orchestral and choral sounds to suggest the music still being made, in the beyond, by those lost music makers.

Scottish composer Anna Meredith wrote one of the year’s most unusual scores for the romantic fantasy “Wicker,” which stars Olivia Colman as a fisherwoman and Alexander Skarsgård as her artificial husband, made for her by a basket weaver in their medieval village.

The entire score is played by just four people: a violist, a cellist, a recorder player and Meredith herself. “I’d much rather start small with a tiny lens, and see what you can do with it, rather than have every sound in the world, where it could just sound like any old thing. You have to really think creatively,” she says.

Directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson reached out to Meredith during shooting (to write music for a wedding scene), and she quickly became part of a team that included several women in key roles (including editor Sofi Marshall). The composer decided that the timeframe and the nature of the story demanded wooden instruments for a “timeless quality.”

Meredith used as many as 10 different recorders, “from tiny little baby ones, only 20 centimeters; lots of ones in the conventional treble tenor range; and some bonkers instruments, including a bass one and a contrabass one which was so tall we had to move to a different recording studio. We had to find one with a skylight to fit the neck of that one, like seven feet tall.”

The recorders represented the fisherwoman and her wicker husband, while the strings (the darker sounds of viola and cello) represented the villagers. “It’s not nice string sounds,” she says, “it’s slithery, nasty sounds. Their sound worlds are, initially, kept quite different, and then the strings sort of ‘infect’ the recorders as the villagers start to impose on their relationship.”

The directors “wanted the score to be bold,” Meredith adds, “and it’s loud as well. The music is upfront. I’m very proud to be part of a film with a strong female story and so many important female elements, both on and off the screen, that have been part of it.”

For “Tenzing,” the untold story of the Nepalese-Indian Sherpa who accompanied Edmund Hillary to the top of Mount Everest in 1953, Norwegian-born, Stockholm-based composer Rebekka Karijord insisted on cultural authenticity. “I felt, early on, that we needed to have a collaboration with Nepalese musicians that isn’t like an exotic tone or a color,” she says. “It had to be a deep collaboration.”

She enlisted a Nepalese spiritual leader and Buddhist nun, Ani Choying Drolma, to contribute traditional Buddhist chants; Nepal’s premier flautist and throat singer Manose Singh; and actress Thinley Lhamo, who plays Tenzing’s wife Dawa in the film and is also a highly regarded singer of Tibetan opera.

Lhamo “has the most amazing voice,” Karijord says. That voice becomes, in a sense, the sound of the mountain itself. “I wanted to have something that could transcend the physical effort, that could pull us into the spiritual aspect, and her voice really solved that for me throughout the score.”

In addition, she had the sound team record a number of unique sounds from the region—yak bells, goat bells, the sound of prayer wheels in the temples, Tibetan singing bowls and gongs—which she and her percussionist sampled and added to her musical library for incorporation into the score.

The film details England’s drive to be the first nation to reach the summit of the world’s tallest peak, Karijord points out. “It needed the big cinematic muscles, a meeting between Western and Eastern. If I could make the mountain, this goddess, beautiful and pristine and dangerous and magnetizing, then we will understand why’re drawn to her—both Tenzing as a little boy growing up at the foot of the mountain, and these Englishmen wanting to conquer it.”

Karijord employed a 40-piece string section from the London Contemporary Orchestra, in part to convey the danger of crevasses, avalanches and rumbles in the ice, along with a handful of woodwind and brass players and a 12-voice choir. Textural elements, such as the sound of breathing, also became a factor in the score.

Regarding the few female composers scoring studio films, Karijord notes that “it’s such a deeply empathetic craft to score films, and it’s a deeply collaborative craft. I know a lot of women who are both very empathetic and collaborative and brave. So I think there should be more of us doing it.”

"3 Body Problem," Netflix's unsettling adaptation of the first book in Chinese author Cixin Liu's epic alien invasion trilogy, "Remembrance of Earth’s Past," made a serious impact on viewers searching for hardcore E.T. drama and now an explosive new trailer for season 2 has just entered our orbit.

This sensational saga about a malevolent interstellar society trying to exist within the unpredictable orbital mechanics of a planet and its triple sun system that forms an Earth-bound armada still has us a bit slack-jawed more than two years after debuting in 2024. Now we're admittedly eager for this shortened 6-episode sophomore outing, which is officially arriving on Jan. 14, 2027.

Delivered by Emmy Award-winning "Game of Thrones" team of David Benioff and D.B. Weiss and "True Blood's" Alexander Woo, "3 Body Problem" season 2 revolves around the combined forces of the Planetary Defense Council as they mount a daring deep space counterattack against the San-Ti.

These Trisolarians are not the friendliest of galactic neighbors, and prior to the all-out invasion their primary goal was to thwart humanity’s ability to create advanced defense weaponry in the four centuries it would take for them to enter our solar system. This time it's more about the next phase of ultimate survival and dire actions taken by anti-alien and pro-alien factions.

Season 2 leaps forward 400 years and focuses on the results of the Wallfacer Project, a secret initiative where chosen individuals worked on solutions in isolation as to not attract the attention of the Trisolarian's omnipresent AI surveillance technology called sophons.

While the debut season was based on Liu's Hugo Award-winning 2008 novel, "The Three-Body Problem," this upcoming Netflix offering will adapt the second book, "The Dark Forest." 2010's "Death's End" closed out the acclaimed sci-fi trilogy.

"So much of season 1 is about the mystery of what's happening," co-creator and co-executive producer David Benioff tells Netflix. "By the time season 2 starts, we have a lot more information. We know there is a hostile alien civilization out there, the San-Ti, and they’re coming our way, and they want our planet for themselves."

Landing on Jan. 14, 2027, "3 Body Problem" season 2's international cast includes returners Jess Hong, Benedict Wong, Jovan Adepo, Eiza González, Liam Cunningham, Marlo Kelly, Sea Shimooka, Saamer Usmani, Alex Sharp and Josh Brener. Joining them are fresh cast members Claudia Doumit, Ellie de Lange, Alfie Allen, David Yip and Jordan Sunshine.
